10579-joe-strong-the-boy-fire-eater-or-t:
Vance Barnum published this circus story in 1916, following Joe Strong, the boy fire-eater, in the most dangerous performance on record. Barnum, author of Joe Strong the Boy Wizard and other Joe Strong books, sets the tale in Sampson Brothers' Circus, where ringmaster Jim Tracy introduces each act with flair.

The vanishing lady opens the book, after dives, clowns, hurrying horses, and ponderous elephants have thrilled the crowd. Joe, in a spotless white silk suit, steps to the center stage to mystify and interest all. Readers get a lively, old-style circus adventure for boys, full of magic, danger, and showmanship.
10776-the-moving-picture-boys-at-panama:
Victor Appleton wrote The Moving Picture Boys at Panama in 1915, sending Joe and his friends to film the great canal. Chapters run from a rescue and a delayed letter through New York and off for Panama, along the canal, into the jungle, and through Culebra Cut. A collision, an emergency dam, a big slide, and Joe's plight raise the stakes.

The boys' camera gives the adventure its shape, as they chase a secret conference and the missing Mr. Alcando. Appleton writes brisk, clean fun for young readers. The book doubles as a boy's-eye view of the Panama Canal in the year it opened.
12169-sakoontala-or-the-lost-ring-an-ind:
Sir Monier Monier-Williams translated Kalidasa Sanskrit drama Sakuntala into English prose and verse, first in 1855, with this eighth edition revised after seven printings. Monier-Williams, Boden Professor of Sanskrit at Oxford, called it India most celebrated drama.

The plot follows King Dushyanta, who meets Sakuntala in a forest hermitage, marries her, and then, under a curse, forgets her until a lost ring restores his memory. Scenes move from hermitage to court to heaven, with lovers, a clown, and a ring found in a fish. The play blends love, duty, and fate in the classical Indian manner. Monier-Williams translation made it a staple of English reading lists, praised as one of the hundred best books.
12790-the-true-woman-a-series-of-discour:
Rev. J. D. Fulton preached these Boston discourses in 1869, setting out a Bible-based view of woman's place. Eve as helpmeet anchors his case: woman blesses the home, shapes morals, and guards faith, while the ballot, he argues, would pull her from that calling. A closing lecture, Woman versus Ballot, states the case against suffrage directly.

Fulton traces woman from creation through the Fall to her work in home, church, and society, warning that power in the home carries heavy duty. His tone is earnest and pastoral, not coarse. The book now reads as a clear record of one side of the nineteenth-century debate over women's rights.
13483-the-drama:
Henry Irving, the great Victorian actor-manager, gathers addresses on the stage in this volume, with a frontispiece by Whistler. He opens at the Philosophical Institution in Edinburgh in November 1881, defending the theatre as a working institution rather than an abstract art praised in empty phrases.

Irving writes on the art of acting, on four great actors, and on the soul of interpretation that no record of stage positions can preserve. An actor must impersonate, not recite, moved by the impulse of being. He praises Betterton for keeping Hamlet alive against witty Restoration comedies, and argues for natural feeling over monotonous, artificial style.
14454-the-doctor-s-dilemma:
Hesba Stretton's 1872 novel sends its hero to the Channel Islands, where a doctor without resources must treat patients on Sark and Guernsey. The story opens with a rough night at sea and a safe haven.

Dr. Martin Dobrée meets a mysterious patient, a rival practitioner, and a young woman whose identity and friends are unknown, while wedding dresses, locks of hair, and stolen letters deepen the plot. Stretton, a popular evangelical novelist, mixes romance with moral earnestness. The novel moves between island scenery and domestic secrets, and it kept Victorian readers turning pages.
15567-an-account-of-the-customs-and-mann:
A French abbot who lived many years as a missionary among the Micmakis and Maricheets wrote this account, printed in London in 1758 from an original French manuscript letter never before published. Several pieces on the savages, Nova Scotia, and North America in general are annexed. The peoples described lived dependent on the government of Cape Breton.

A preface draws on a French ministry memorial of April 1751, which counted about six hundred fighting men before the last war, in villages on Cape Breton island and nearby shores. The letter itself describes customs, manners, government, and mission life, while later pieces accuse French priests of seducing deserters back to French allegiance. The account is a colonial document, biased in its politics, yet valuable for its firsthand detail on Mi'kmaq life.
16199-memoirs-of-the-author-of-a-vindica:
William Godwin published these memoirs in London in 1798, just after the death of Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. Godwin, her husband, argues that giving the public an account of a person of eminent merit is a duty of survivors, since calumny and misrepresentation so often follow the dead. His memoir opens with her years from 1759 to 1775 and follows her life in chapters.

The book is both a love letter and a defense, frank about Wollstonecraft's mind, work, and private sorrows. It shocked some readers and moved others, and it shaped her fame for generations. Modern readers meet here the founding text of feminist biography, written by the man who knew her best.
18239-the-road-to-mandalay-a-tale-of-bur:
B. M. Croker published this tale of Burma with Cassell in October 1917, with reprints in December 1917 and in March and May 1918. The book is dedicated to Lt. Col. A. E. Congdon of the Royal Munster Fusiliers. Its early chapters, Blinds Down, What Hannah Said, and The Closed House, set a household mystery before the road east opens.

Later chapters send the heroine bound for Burma aboard the Blankshire, to a land of promise, a Burmese hostess, and the meeting of east and west. A chummery, a Chinese shop, a play, and a cocaine den mark the darker turns, with an approaching dread near the close. Readers get an Anglo-Indian romance of travel, society, and danger, told from the deck of a steamer to the streets of Mandalay.
18799-the-growth-of-english-drama:
Arnold Wynne's Oxford study, first published in 1914, traces English drama from its church beginnings to the Elizabethan stage. It opens with the tableaux and Latin services through which clergy on the Continent first acted out Bible scenes, then follows English miracle plays, moralities, and interludes toward full comedy and tragedy.

Later chapters treat Lyly, Greene, Peele, and Nash in comedy, and Lodge, Kyd, Marlowe, and Arden of Feversham in tragedy. An appendix covers the Elizabethan stage itself. Wynne writes for readers who want the whole line of growth in one short book, from altar steps to a public theatre with its own craft.
19171-the-moving-picture-girls-or-first-:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this 1914 Moving Picture Girls tale about Ruth and Alice and their first appearances in photo dramas. The sisters, left without a mother, seek work in films, where Russ Dalwood apologises, troubles return, and a new proposition changes Alice's mind. A front piece shows them holding the stage alone.

A man bursts through their hall door, Ruth fears fighting in the halls, and Alice calms her, noting Russ across the hall and the strength she once praised. Danger and pluck mix with studio life. Young readers get a lively girls' tale of early movies, sisterhood, and courage.
1955-the-darrow-enigma:
Melvin L. Severy's Darrow Enigma is built as a set of episodes: The Darkened Room, The Sealed Document, Rama Ragobah. The Parallel, each opening a new corner of a mystery. A woman half-closes her eyes and leans back in a man's arms. The scene, half faint and half trust, sets the tone for a novel that works through suggestion rather than shock.

Severy writes the detective story as a puzzle of documents and identities, with a hero who must study seals, rooms, and faces to find a murderer. The book is a period piece of the 1890s, earnest and intricate. Its charm lies in its structure: four episodes, each a locked box, each opening onto the next.
2029-lahoma:
John Breckenridge Ellis sets a frontier novel in the Oklahoma country, where a child, a prisoner under oath, and a band of rough men set the plot in motion. Brick, a young man of the plains, must choose between loyalty, love, and survival. Ellis wrote frontier tales for young readers, and Lahoma mixes adventure with a plea for kindness to strangers.

Chapters carry the story from flight and a mysterious guest to fences, a mob, and a final stand, with Lahoma at its heart. Ellis writes of the border country with warmth, and the book blends adventure, romance, and a plea for fair dealing. The Oklahoma setting matters, since fences, claims, and new towns were still fresh facts when Ellis wrote.
21768-a-desert-drama:
Tourists on the Nile steamer Korosko sail from Shellal on February 13, 1895, in this adventure novel by A. Conan Doyle. The flat-bottomed boat is bound for Wady Halfa, past the first cataract of the Nile. Doyle frames the tale as a true incident long kept out of the papers for private and political reasons. He builds it from sworn statements, letters, and a secret inquiry at Cairo.

The pleasure trip turns to desert drama when danger closes on the party far from help. Doyle, already famous for Sherlock Holmes, brings the same tight craft to a tale of capture and rescue. Colonel Cochrane, Miss Adams of Boston, and Captain Archer of the Camel Corps anchor his cast of witnesses.
2293-a-new-england-girlhood-outlined-fro:
Lucy Larcom remembers growing up in Beverly, Massachusetts, and working in the Lowell mills as a girl. A New England Girlhood traces her path from a seaside childhood to the mill town's boarding houses, libraries, and literary circles, where young women read poetry between shifts. Larcom writes with warmth and a reformer's eye.

Her memoir matters as a firsthand record of mill girls' inner lives, not just their labor. She recalls teachers, books, and friendships that shaped her into a poet and editor. Readers of American social history will find a gentle, vivid witness.
23544-glaucoma:
Willis O. Nance and Wesley Hamilton Peck edited this nineteen fourteen symposium on glaucoma, papers given at a meeting of the Chicago Ophthalmological Society in November nineteen thirteen. Contributors include Edward Jackson and other leading eye surgeons of the day, each speaking from clinic and college.

The papers take up the nature, signs, and care of glaucoma, a disease of raised pressure in the eye that can steal sight, with debate on surgery, drugs, and diagnosis. Printed by the Chicago Medical Book Company, the volume suits doctors and students of eye history. Modern readers should treat its treatments as history, not guidance, while valuing the book as a record of how eye care stood on the eve of modern methods.
24253-folkways-a-study-of-the-sociologic:
William Graham Sumner, professor of political and social science at Yale University, wrote this study of custom, published by Ginn and Company in 1906. Its full title names its subject: the sociological importance of usages, manners, customs, mores, and morals. Sumner opens with words from Castiglione, Hamlet, and Coriolanus on the monster custom, which eats all sense yet clothes fair actions in a livery.

The book argues that use, rather than reason, introduces new things among us and does away with old ones. Folkways, Sumner holds, shape what a people calls right long before philosophers reason about it. Readers get a founding work of American sociology, plain in aim and wide in examples.
25088-famous-sea-fights-from-salamis-to-:
John Richard Hale's Famous Sea Fights, published in Boston in 1911, retells decisive naval battles from ancient Salamis to modern Tsu-shima. Hale, writing for general readers, pairs narrative history with thirteen illustrations and seventeen battle plans that show how fleets moved.

Chapters follow galleys, sailing ships, and steam warships across two thousand years, stressing seamanship, gunnery, and command decisions over mere lists of ships. The Spanish Armada campaign gets close treatment, including English skill at sail and gun and Spanish mismanagement. The book remains a lively survey of war at sea.
2570-two-men-of-sandy-bar-a-drama:
Bret Harte turned his California tales into a stage play with this drama of Sandy Bar, a mining town full of prodigals, gamblers, and lost sons. The cast lists Sandy, son of Alexander Morton, John Oakhurst posing as the prodigal, Colonel Starbottle as legal adviser, and Don Jose with his daughter Jovita.

Old Morton, a detective, an Australian convict, and a rancho major domo crowd the action as identities swap and old debts surface. Harte writes for the stage with broad humor and sudden feeling. The play shows how his frontier types, born in stories, could swagger, scheme, and reconcile under the footlights.
26595-the-condition-and-tendencies-of-te:
Arthur Henry Chamberlain, a professor of education at Throop Polytechnic Institute in Pasadena, published this survey at Syracuse in 1908. He asks how far a country's factory and trade growth rests on technical schools. He finds Germany in the forefront of putting science to work in the arts. Railroads, bridges, water supply, electric vehicles, and fine tools all show that training at work.

Chamberlain sorts the German system in sections, from continuation schools, the Fortbildungsschulen, and trade schools, the Fachschulen, to higher technical schools, the Technische Hochschulen. Secondary technical schools and schools of industrial art get their own sections too. A list of books closes the study. It remains a clear snapshot of a system other nations studied and envied.
26783-the-story-of-the-kearsarge-and-ala:
This short narrative of the Kearsarge and the Alabama was published at San Francisco by Henry Payot and Company in 1868, printed by Edward Bosqui and Company on Clay Street. Its author published from the want of a popular, detailed, and yet concise account of the engagement between the two vessels.

On Sunday, June 12, 1864, the United States steamer Kearsarge lay anchored in the Scheldt off Flushing, Holland. A telegram from Minister Dayton at Paris announced that the notorious Alabama had arrived at Cherbourg. Captain Winslow sailed at once, called at Dover for dispatches, and appeared off Cherbourg Breakwater. Captain Semmes declared his intention to fight, writing that he hoped his arrangements would not detain him beyond the next evening. The battle that followed left decks covered with blood and gun crews renewed four times.
27275-the-angel-of-thought-and-other-poe:
Ethel Allen Murphy wrote these short poems after looking at paintings by old masters, and the book pairs each poem with the picture that prompted it. Fra Angelico, Botticelli, and Albrecht Dürer supply the images, from an angel of thought to Madonnas and scenes from the life of the Virgin. Copyrighted in 1908 and published in Boston in 1909, the volume is dedicated to Murphy's friend and teacher Anna J. Hamilton.

The poems stay close to what the paintings show: angels with lifted faces, a wondering mother, a mourning mother, and a loving Christ child. Short sonnets on the Annunciation and the Visitation sit beside a prayer for followers of ideal beauty. Readers who like art and verse together get a gentle guide to famous religious pictures, read through one poet's eyes.
28266-the-duke-s-motto-a-melodrama:
Justin Huntly McCarthy's The Duke's Motto, published by Harper and Brothers in August 1908, is a melodrama in novel form, built around Lagardere, hero of French swashbuckling romance. McCarthy dedicates the book in French to Victorien Sardou, true creator of Lagardere, and says he wrote it for actor Lewis Waller. Words, he admits, replace action, scenery, and costumes.

The story follows Lagardere, peer of d'Artagnan and Cyrano, through duels, disguises, and honourable revenge. McCarthy, author of If I Were King and Seraphica, writes in the high romantic style. Readers of cloak-and-sword tales will find the melodrama brisk and earnest.
30024-the-fisher-boy-urashima:
B. H. Chamberlain wrote The Fisher-Boy Urashima as number eight in the Japanese Fairy Tales series, printed in London and Sydney by Griffith Farran and Company. Long ago, on Japan's sea coast, lived a young fisherman called Urashima, kind-hearted and skilled with rod and line.

 Urashima reasons that a fish would do for dinner just as well, in fact better. Why should he kill the poor creature and cut short nine hundred and ninety-nine more years of enjoyment? His mother would not like such cruelty, he decides, and he throws the tortoise back into the sea. As he sleeps in his boat on a hot summer afternoon, a beautiful girl rises from beneath the waves and says she is the daughter of the Sea-God.
30064-peeps-at-many-lands-burma:
R. Talbot Kelly introduces Burma to young readers in eleven chapters, with twelve full-page colour pictures drawn by the author himself. Rangoon, the Irrawaddy river, village life, town life, field work, and the forest each get a chapter, closing with temples and religion. A sketch map opens the book, and plates show pagoda steps, a rest house, a market place, and the golden monastery at Mandalay.

Adam and Charles Black published the London volume in 1908, in the Peeps at Many Lands series, and Kelly writes as a traveler who sketched what he saw. His tone is warm and simple, aimed at school-age readers curious about a far land. The book now reads as both a period travel primer and a record of how Edwardian Britain pictured Burma to its children.
30620-two-new-pelycosaurs-from-the-lower:
Richard C. Fox writes Two New Pelycosaurs from the Lower Permian of Oklahoma. It appears in University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume twelve, number six, pages 297 to 307, with six figures, published 21 May 1962. Editors include E. Raymond Hall, Henry S. Fitch, and Theodore H. Eaton Jr.

Fox studied early Permian fissure material from a limestone quarry near Fort Sill, Oklahoma, and found several small, tooth-bearing pelycosaur pieces. The paper names and describes two new forms from those fragments, placing them in early reptile history. It serves paleontologists and students of Permian life with concise, specimen-based science.
31500-the-position-of-woman-in-primitive:
C. Gasquoine Hartley's The Position of Woman in Primitive Society, a study of the matriarchy, examines women's place in early societies. Hartley, author of The Truth About Woman and books on Spanish art and Spain, organizes the work in two parts. It moves from the evidence for mother-centered social forms to their meaning for the history of the family. The book belongs to the early feminist anthropology of its day, arguing that women's early status was higher than later ages allowed.

Hartley draws on travel reports, custom, and myth to build her case, and she writes for general readers as well as students. Later anthropology has revised much of this picture, but the book remains interesting as a statement of its moment. Readers will find a bold, readable argument about sex, power, and the deep past.
33232-bert-wilson-at-panama:
J. W. Duffield's boys' adventure opens in wild country, where Dick Trent faces armed men and a plot that soon widens far past one hold-up. Bert Wilson and his friends are drawn into a chase, a captured sentry, and a scheme led by the bandit El Tigre. The action then shifts to Panama, where the great canal, a treacherous bog, and a deserted city set the stage for fresh peril.

The sixteen chapters move briskly from pursuits and escapes to a plan to cut wires and foil a plot against the canal zone. Duffield writes for young readers, with brave comrades, clear villains, and danger that is met head-on. First printed in 1914, the book pairs frontier daring with the marvel of the canal, and ends with the boys' scheme undone and their foes stopped.
3361-letters-to-his-son-complete-on-the-:
This volume gathers the Earl of Chesterfield's letters to his son complete, from 1746 to the end of the correspondence. An editor's note opens the book, explaining old style and new style dates. The abbreviations mark the Julian calendar used in England against the Gregorian calendar standard in Europe, a gap of eleven days in the mid eighteenth century. That key unlocks the whole correspondence.

Across the years the letters teach a single art: becoming a man of the world and a gentleman. Study, languages, manners, morals, and diplomacy pass in order, as a boy becomes a diplomat and a father becomes old. Readers get Chesterfield whole here, without hunting volume by volume, in the fullest form of a classic of worldly wisdom.
34111-politics-of-alabama:
J. C. Manning's 1893 book Politics of Alabama takes up the famous Kolb-Jones contest for governor, fought to the state vote of August 1, 1892. Manning, writing from the Populist side, charges the ruling Democrats with machine rule, harsh campaign methods, and unfair counts.

Eight chapters move from the contest itself to party prejudice, the troubles of the sixties, and the rise of the Populists, whom Manning sees as sure to win. He dedicates the book to Alabamians who demand a free ballot and a fair count, and his plea is for honest rule over party power.
34677-red-eagle-and-the-wars-with-the-cr:
George Cary Eggleston tells a frontier life in Red Eagle and the Wars with the Creek Indians of Alabama, printed in New York with copyright in 1878. Dodd Mead made the book, in a run of famous American Indians. A plate shows Red Eagle's leap.

His preface is frank about sources. A work of this kind makes no pretension to originality in its materials, he says. All that is here related is to be found in books. Yet no one book is devoted solely to the history of the Creek war, he notes, or to the life of William Weatherford, the Red Eagle. The matter was gathered from many sources, some long out of print. Parton's life of Andrew Jackson stands in his list of books consulted.
35107-cruise-and-captures-of-the-alabama:
Albert M Goodrich recounts a famous raider in Cruise and Captures of the Alabama, published at Minneapolis in 1906. His preface lists rich sources: the naval records of the Rebellion from both sides, and Captain Semmes's diary grown into a memoir. Diaries of the ship's officers and the long report of the Geneva Tribunal of Arbitration add more. Consular reports add their share.

The first chapter, England and the Blockade, sets the scene: a vast Yankee carrying trade, then news in October 1862 that the Alabama was burning Northern ships. Goodrich weighs the charge that she was a mere pirate. Naval readers get a sourced account.
35940-the-golden-galleon-being-a-narrati:
Robert Leighton wrote The Golden Galleon, a tale of Master Gilbert Oglander in the great sea fight off Flores. Leighton had writ Olaf the Glorious and The Pilots of Pomona. William Rainey drew the pictures. Blackie and Son issued the book at London, Glasgow, and Bombay. Review lines from the Times and Spectator head the work.

Gilbert fought under Sir Richard Grenville in the year 1591. He sailed on Her Majesty's ship the Revenge. The fight off Flores in the Azores is the famed last stand of that ship. Review lines call the tale well built and lively. Its chief merit lies in the telling, one says. The book gives a fine picture of life in England on land and sea in the days of Queen Elizabeth, says one more. Sea risk and honor drive the youth tale.
36529-mr-punch-at-the-play-humours-of-mu:
Mr Punch at the Play is an anthology of theatre humour from Punch magazine. Hammerton edited the Punch Library of Humour, which gathered the best of the magazine from 1841 on. This volume treats the humours of music and the drama. It holds one hundred and forty illustrations.

The drawings come from Charles Keene, Phil May, George du Maurier, Bernard Partridge, and a dozen more of Punch's masters. One caption shows an actor declaring his mind made up, while a voice from the gallery asks about his face. The editor notes that Punch drew much fun from French dramas and from audiences who feigned pleasure in a tongue they did not know. The book is a seat in the stalls of Victorian comedy, jokes and all.
36590-the-english-stage-being-an-account:
The English Stage, being an account of the Victorian drama, is a theatre history by Augustin Filon, Englished from the French by Frederic Whyte and issued at London in 1897. A playwright of the day provides an introduction. Filon's other works, in French, are listed at the front. The contents open with a glance back at the years from 1820 to 1830.

Kean and Macready, the strolling player, and the critics fill the first chapter's heads. Sheridan Knowles and his Virginius, and Douglas Jerrold with his comedies, stand among its names. The fall of the privileged theatres and the rescue of the drama by men of letters close that chapter. Bulwer Lytton's plays, The Lady of Lyons and Richelieu among them, end the list. A Frenchman's cool, clear view of the English stage is the book's distinction.
37558-a-catalogue-of-sculpture-in-the-de:
A Catalogue of Sculpture in the Department of Greek and Roman Antiquities is a British Museum volume by Smith. Smith served as an assistant in that department of the museum in London. Volume one was printed by order of the trustees in eighteen ninety two. Its preface, by Murray, sets out the ground the volume covers in detail.

The book treats the sculptures of the archaic period of Greek art. It also covers the Parthenon and other Athenian buildings in the store. Remains of the temple at Phigaleia and the Greek reliefs follow in the scheme. Some works made in Roman times are included as copies of Greek originals. Much of the Athens section keeps text from Newton's guide to the Elgin Room. New research is added, and views on the reliefs are briefly set out.
3823-thelma:
Marie Corelli sets this romance in Norway, in the land of the midnight sun. The book opens at midnight without darkness, as the unwearied sun stands over the Altenfjord and turns its waters bronze, copper, silver, and azure. Thelma, the heroine, moves through this radiant world with a lover, Philip Errington, while Sigurd, a jealous rival, haunts the falls and cliffs.

A later scene finds Errington bewildered after a narrow escape, asking where Sigurd has gone, while a friend laughs off the danger with a trembling lip. Corelli writes in high romantic colors, with fjords, light, and passion in full flood. Readers who like sweeping love stories will find Thelma a grand and sentimental tale, with Norway itself as a second heroine.
38815-prowling-about-panama:
George A Miller's Prowling About Panama, copyrighted in 1919 and issued by the Abingdon Press, is dedicated to the young people of the Epworth Leagues of the California Conference. Alice and A W Best illustrated the book from photographs by the author himself. A foreword opens the prowling at page 11 of the contents.

The contents promise a wide prowling. Chapters follow the trail of the pirates, a city of ghosts, the spell of the jungle, and the interior. Then come economic waste, progress, and the Panama Canal itself. The last chapters look at knowing our neighbors, the Latin-American heart, the Caribbean world, and prowling into the future.
39187-sop-s-fables-embellished-with-one-:
Æsop's Fables, printed at the Chiswick Press by Whittingham in 1814, is embellished with one hundred and eleven emblematical devices. The contents run in the old order: the Cock and the Jewel first, then the Wolf and the Lamb, the Lion and the Four Bulls, and the Frog and the Fox. The famous ones are all here.

The Lion and the Mouse, the Dog in the Manger, the Ant and the Grasshopper, the Crow and the Pitcher, and the Country Mouse and the City Mouse stand in the list. So do the Oak and the Reed, the Wind and the Sun, the Frogs Desiring a King, and the Hare and the Tortoise. Editions like this one were made for the drawing room as much as the nursery.
4049-piccolissima:
A children's fantasy follows a little girl named Piccolissima who finds herself stared at by a fly with ten or twelve thousand eyes. The fly's gaze confuses her, until she recalls that behind all those mirrored faces there is only one power of seeing.

The tale turns on wonder and good sense, as Piccolissima steadies herself with reason in a strange, small world. Written in the fanciful manner of Victorian children's stories, it mixes marvel with a gentle lesson. Young readers who like tiny heroes and odd, kind magic will enjoy this short, curious tale.
40958-the-seaman-s-friend-containing-a-t:
Dana wrote this handbook for sailors, in a fifth edition published by Groom at Boston in 1847. A treatise on practical seamanship with plates fills the first part of the book. A dictionary of sea terms, the customs of the merchant service and the laws of a master's duties follow in the full title.

Dana entered the work for copyright in 1841, the year after 'Two Years Before the Mast' made his name. He addresses sea-faring persons, owners, insurers and judges in maritime law alike in his contents. Knots, rigging, cargo rules and a young sailor's legal rights fill a friend indeed for men before the mast.
41220-military-career-of-napoleon-the-gr:
Montgomery Gibbs wrote this anecdotal military history of Napoleon, published at Chicago in 1895. Its subtitle promises the campaigns of the Man of Destiny with battlefield anecdotes told by the famous marshals and generals of the First Empire.

In his preface Gibbs protests that a passing Napoleonic wave did not cause the book; it rests on years of study, including the marshals' memoirs published long after their deaths. His aim is not technical: to picture Napoleon as his soldiers knew him, on the field and round the campfire. A verse from Thackeray fronts the book. Readers get the Little Corporal through the eyes of the men who marched with him.
41680-civil-war-and-reconstruction-in-al:
Civil War and Reconstruction in Alabama, by Walter Fleming, is a state history. Columbia University Press issued the book in nineteen o five. Fleming taught history at West Virginia University when the work appeared. He gives the book to his wife Mary Boyd Fleming inside.

Part one covers the era of sectional clash before the war years. Chapters treat the people of Alabama, slavery fights, and party splits. William Lowndes Yancey and the growth of secession feeling earn close study. Unionists won in eighteen fifty one and two, the contents note. Later chapters trace the secession convention and the ordinance itself in detail.
42865-english-conferences-of-ernest-rena:
Ernest Renan's English Conferences gathers five lectures delivered in London in April 1880, translated by Clara Erskine Clement and published at Boston the same year. Four Hibbert lectures treat Rome and Christianity: Rome as the work's true author, the legend of Peter and Paul, the growth of church authority, and Rome as capital of Catholicism. A fifth lecture, on Marcus Aurelius, was given before the Royal Institution.

Renan opens by thanking the Hibbert Foundation, endowed by Robert Hibbert some thirty years earlier to aid enlightened Christianity. He argues that the pursuit of truth, approved in every other field, must not be softened when it turns to religion.
43060-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The McKinley-to-Ma slice of the eleventh Britannica opens, like its fellows, with the transcriber's list of corrected misprints, and the quoted lines sample the articles inside. Madison, James gives a date: on December 26, 1785, Jefferson's bill for religious freedom in Virginia, brought in by Madison, was passed. Madras names its colleges, the agriculture school at Coimbatore and the teachers' college at Saidapet among them.

Magnetism fills much of the list. One note gives the ratio of magnetization to magnetizing force holding steady at 6.4 in weak fields. Another corrects a load at which the pull peaks, and a third a change of properties at a critical heat. Terrestrial Magnetism closes the sample, tying the year's range of the needle to Wolf's sun-spot count.
43075-a-civil-servant-in-burma:
Herbert Thirkell White wrote A Civil Servant in Burma, for Arnold at London in 1913. Pictures fill the book, one of them a Buddha's foot in stone. White gives the book to his wife, who shared his Burma life. That sharing ran for more than thirty-two years, the dedication says. Contents open with a retrospect and some comparisons, then early years.

First impressions, a first subdivision, and the secretariat fill the early chapters. Burmese life and character, and frontier duty, take their turns. The taking of Mandalay and the early days there stand at the center. A first year after the annexation and a few words on Buddhism follow. Service under Crosthwaite from 1887 to 1890, the Shan states, and a boundary commission close the tale. White gives an official's Burma from inside the machine.
43490-the-social-significance-of-the-mod:
Emma Goldman published The Social Significance of the Modern Drama with Richard G Badger at Boston in 1914. Her foreword calls Ibsen, Strindberg, Hauptmann, Tolstoy, Shaw, and Galsworthy the social iconoclasts of the age. Such drama, she says, is dynamite under superstition and the pillars of society.

Chapters work through the Scandinavian drama first: A Doll's House, Ghosts, and An Enemy of Society. German plays follow, from Hauptmann's Weavers to Wedekind's Awakening of Spring. French, English, and Irish sections treat Brieux, Shaw, Galsworthy, Yeats, and others. Goldman's measure is plain: a play counts when it helps men and women throw off the dead weight of the past.
44640-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
The World's Greatest Books, volume seventeen, on poetry and drama, was issued under joint editors Arthur Mee and Hammerton, founder and editor respectively of the Book of Knowledge and Harmsworth's Universal Encyclopaedia. The volume gives the great works in condensed form, each with its story and leading scenes.

Goethe's Goetz von Berlichingen and Iphigenia in Tauris open the volume, continued from the volume before. Gogol's Inspector-General, Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer, and Heine's Atta Troll follow. Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, Horace's poems, and three plays of Hugo come next, then Ibsen's Master Builder and Pillars of Society. Jonson, Juvenal, Klopstock, Lessing, Longfellow, and Lucretius lead on to Marlowe, Martial, and Massinger. Milton fills the last long stretch before Moliere, with Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, and Samson Agonistes.
44880-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons' Popular Science Monthly for May 1899 is the first number of volume fifty-five of a great American science magazine. William Jay Youmans edited it, in the line of its founder, his brother Edward. A portrait of William Pengelly, the geologist, stands at the front. The lead piece is Alaska and the Klondike, by Angelo Heilprin, professor of geology at Philadelphia. Its first part runs in by the White Pass and out by the Chilkoot.

Two years back, Heilprin notes, the names Dawson and Klondike were unknown to the world. Now crowds press to that new Eldorado at the Arctic Circle's edge. Some take fortune, many take shattered hope. Dawson sits where the Klondike meets the Yukon river. The monthly carried science to the general reader each month. This number catches the gold rush at its height.
45210-legends-of-the-pike-s-peak-region-:
Ernest Whitney, assisted by Alexander and with illustrations by Parrish, gathered these legends of the Pike's Peak region for a Denver publisher in 1892. The subtitle calls them the sacred myths of the Manitou. Whitney's opening argument is general: the myths and legends of early nations give the truest exponents of their character. The songs of a people are stronger than their laws, and a bit of folk lore may teach more than chapters of history.

Scotland is his proof. A century ago it was England's byword for dullness, until Scott drew aside the veil and the land of mountain and flood became dear to all. Tourists then complained that Colorado, grander than the Alps, had no traditions. Whitney answers that the traditions exist and only want gathering. The plates name them: the healing fountain, the great dragon, the temple of the lesser spirits, and the wigwam of the Manitou.
45915-the-pacification-of-burma:
The Pacification of Burma is Sir Charles Crosthwaite's account of his years as Chief Commissioner of Burma, from 1887 to 1890. Edward Arnold of London published it in 1912, with illustrations and maps.

Twenty-three chapters run from the administration of Burma to Mandalay and the dacoits. Disarmament, a visit to Bhamo, and trouble with the Wuntho Sawbwa follow. Military forces give place to police, and a police force is gradually built. Chapters treat the Shan States, the Karennis, and the trans-Salween country. The Chins receive two chapters, ending with the Chin-Lushai campaign. Illustrations show the Mandalay palace, a frontier stockade, and village headmen in consultation. The narrative opens in 1852, with Lord Dalhousie's proclamation annexing Pegu.
49080-closing-in-marines-in-the-seizure-:
Closing In: Marines in the Seizure of Iwo Jima, by Colonel Joseph Alexander of the Marine Corps, retired, belongs to the Marines in World War II Commemorative Series. Sidebars run beside the narrative: the Japanese commander, the flag raising photograph, the 320mm spigot mortar, flame tanks, and the rocket detachments among them.

The chapters move from assault preparations through D-Day and Suribachi to the drive north and the bitter end. A closing chapter weighs Iwo Jima's costs, gains, and legacies. The narrative opens on Sunday, 4 March 1945, ending the invasion's second week. The assault troops of the third, fourth, and fifth Marine divisions were spent. Their fighting strength had fallen to dangerous levels. The flag had gone up on Mount Suribachi ten days before. The landing force had already taken 13,000 casualties, 3,000 of them dead. Ahead lay the main Japanese defences, uphill.
49319-an-essay-on-contagious-diseases-mo:
An Essay on Contagious Diseases is a doctors treatise by Wintringham, more bent on the small pox, the red rash ill, and the foul fevers of rot and pest. It was printed at York in the early eighteen twenties, for sale at York and at a shop in a famed row of London.

Its first words set out its plan in full. The aim of this wee book, it says, is to draw out the causes and lay plain the shows of some of the most death full ills that smite man. That aim needs no plea, it holds. The less so as some of those ills rage now with rare force, and the land is each day in dread of a vast pest. He seeks to cut these ills to the plain frame of one lore.
49473-the-little-ball-o-fire-or-the-life: The Little Ball o' Fire, a tale of the life and adventures of John Marston, is a novel by James, the popular historical romancer. It reached readers as volume 15 of the new illustrated edition of his works, issued in parts from 1844. The hosted pages open with the publisher's list of that edition, from The Gipsy and Mary of Burgundy to this tale on January 1, 1848. Readers get a period novel in the dress its first buyers saw.
49561-from-peking-to-mandalay-a-journey-:
From Peking to Mandalay is a travel book by Johnston, a district officer and magistrate at Weihaiwei and a member of the Royal Asiatic Society. John Murray published it in London in 1908, with a map and illustrations. Its subtitle promises a journey from north China to Burma through Tibetan Ssuch'uan and Yunnan.

The chapters trace the road stage by stage. From Peking the traveller descends to Ichang and passes the Yangtse gorges to Wan-hsien and Ch'êng-tu. Two chapters climb Mount Omei and explain Chinese Buddhism. Then the road runs west to Tachienlu, over the Yalung river to Muli, and south through Yung-ning and Li-chiang to Tali-fu. A chapter on the ethnology of the Chinese far west follows. From Bhamo the journey ends at Mandalay. Appendixes give vocabularies and the full itinerary, day by day.
50573-correspondence-and-report-from-his:
A British blue book of February 1904 prints letters and a report on the rule of the Congo Free State, laid before both houses of Parliament. The chief piece is the report of Roger Casement, the consul at Boma, on his trip into the inner Congo and the state of the native folk there. It runs from page 21 of the volume.

Front letters include a note from Lord Cromer on Congo posts at Kiro and Lado, where few natives were to be seen. The Congo government's reply to a British note of August is also printed, with a British memo in answer. The book is a key state paper in the world outcry over Congo rule under King Leopold.
5070-the-doctor-s-dilemma:
George Bernard Shaw's Doctor's Dilemma opens on a forenoon in a doctor's consulting room, where Redpenny, a medical student of unknown Christian name and no importance, sits at work. He devils for the doctor by answering letters, acting as domestic laboratory assistant, and making himself indispensable generally, in return for informal apprenticeship and affiliation with a leader of the profession.

Redpenny is not proud and will do anything asked without reservation of dignity, if asked in a fellow-creaturely way, wide-eyed, ready, credulous, and friendly. Shaw's comedy of medicine follows from that consulting room. Readers get a play about doctors, patients, and the dilemma of whom to save, argued with Shavian brilliance.
52226-a-prisoner-of-the-khaleefa-twelve-:
Charles Neufeld tells how he spent twelve years a prisoner of the Khaleefa at Omdurman, in a book published in London in 1899 with portraits and plans. He set out for Kordofan as a merchant and was betrayed by his guides in the desert.

The contents trace the trap: dervishes sighted at Selima Wells, a fight, capture, looting, and cross-questioning as a supposed spy. Later come Dongola, the road to Omdurman, his first meeting with Slatin, chains, torture, and a mock execution. Neufeld dedicates the book to public opinion. Readers get a famous captivity narrative from inside the Mahdist state, ending only with its fall.
52582-drake-or-the-transfer-of-the-tride:
Drake, or The Transfer of the Trident, a National Drama, by William MacOubrey, was printed in London in 1876, for the author. MacOubrey was a barrister of the Middle Temple. Lines from Isaiah head the play, on a way in the sea and isles waiting on God arm.

The persons list is large. Sir Francis Drake stands first, with the Earl of Leicester, Lord Howard of Effingham, and Cecil. The Spanish ambassador Mendoza, Sir John Hawkins, and Sir Edward Horsey appear. So do spies, sailors, Spaniards, Indians, and Queen Elizabeth herself. In a preface To the Anglo-Saxon Race, MacOubrey says his first object was to thank providence for the might of that race. Readers get a patriotic verse drama of Drake and sea power.
52680-the-caillaux-drama:
John Raphael wrote this account of the Caillaux affair, published by Max Goschen at London in 1914, with photographs of the law courts, the funeral, and the prison cell. Late on Monday afternoon, March 16, 1914, a rumor fired imaginations all over Paris like a train of gunpowder. People in newspaper offices, cafes, and clubs asked whether the news could be true.

The news was that the wife of Joseph Caillaux, the finance minister, had shot Gaston Calmette, editor of the Figaro, in his own office. Raphael follows the drama through her cell, number twelve at Saint Lazare, the husband's examination, and the Figaro's campaign against him. Chapters on the Ton Jo letter, the Agadir affair, and the Rochette case fill in the politics behind the shooting.
54162-the-new-english-canaan-of-thomas-m:
The New English Canaan of Thomas Morton is a seventeenth-century work printed at Boston in 1883 for the Prince Society. Charles Francis Adams the younger supplied introductory matter and notes. Only two hundred fifty copies were printed. Morton of Merry-Mount gets a memoir of nearly a hundred pages before his book begins.

A bibliography follows the memoir, and then the work itself. Its first book treats the origin of the natives, their manners and customs. The second describes the beauty of the country. The third describes the people of New England as Morton found them. The edition preserves a rival view of the colony, set against the Puritan accounts that condemned its author.
54647-sam-steele-s-adventures-in-panama:
Hugh Fitzgerald, a captain, wrote Sam Steele Adventures in Panama, a tale put out at Chicago in 1907. Howard Heath made the first paint works for the plates. A plate at the front shows a bold escape from a tight spot. The tale opens with a plea that Sam takes on a sea trip of great risk.

A queer guest, a car that turns to a boat, and a wreck mark the first third. A dead man tale and the land of the San Blas folk raise the stakes. Names like Nalig-Nad and Princess Ilalah give the tale its tropic hue. War is called, a vale is sought, and a man who makes arrows joins the cast. The princess is lost, a rescue is tried, and a spear thrust tests the band. A turn coat and a last trip out of Panama close the list of parts.
54815-yankee-boys-in-japan-or-the-young-:
Henry Harrison Lewis wrote Yankee Boys in Japan, or The Young Merchants of Yokohama, published by Street and Smith in 1903. The front picture shows Nattie falling through space with a cry on his lips. Chapter one sets him in a Yokohama office on a July afternoon, at a bamboo desk over an account book.

Nattie is a youth of not more than nineteen, with puckered eyes, wrinkles, and a firm, resolute chin. When he rises, his halting gait shows that one leg is shorter than the other. His friend Grant moves through the contents beside Mori and a man named Mr Black, facing an attack of ronins, a struggle in a warehouse, and a wrestling match. Later chapters bring pursuit, a tragedy in a tunnel, flashing swords, and a cry of brotherhood. Readers get a dime-novel adventure of American boys trading, and fighting, in treaty-port Japan.
55457-a-creature-of-the-night-an-italian:
Fergus Hume wrote a mystery novel set in Italy, held under copyright in 1891, and gave it to a friend in memory of Italian idling that spring. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab and other tales of crime. Verse at the front tells of a thing born of night, with vampire wings, sent to curse and blight.

Chapter one, The Ghoul, opens at Verona in a summer of the late century, where the teller had adventure come to him unasked. Eighteen chapters bring a feast of ghosts, a haunted palace, and the phantom of Lucrezia Borgia. A marchese, a voice in the darkness, and a new Lazarus fill the later run.
56964-the-quarterly-of-the-oregon-histor:
The Oregon Historical Society launched its quarterly with this issue, volume one, number one, dated March 1900. James Robertson opens with a long study of how political authority and commonwealth government began in Oregon. Thomas Condon follows with a piece on how pioneer settlement in Oregon was shaped by selection among settlers.

Documents and reminiscence fill the rest of the number. Wyeth's Oregon expeditions are recalled through a piece on historic houses and roads near Boston. Lyman presents the memories of Matthieu, a pioneer voice in his own words. Letters of John McLoughlin and Wyeth appear among the printed documents at the back.
57062-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang for June 1921, volume two number twenty one, came out at Robbinsdale, Minnesota, at two dollars fifty a year. It's coming, the front cries: a laugh, a sigh, a smile, a tear, a giggle, a sob. Full page copies of the Whiz Bang girls in sepia colors are promised. The winter annual, Pedigreed Follies of 1921 to 1922, is advertised for October.

All new jokes, jests, and jingles fill the annual, with Captain Billy's advice to the lovelorn and smokehouse poetry. The Blue Velvet Band, The Face on the Barroom Floor, Toledo Slim, and Lasca are reprinted among the best red blooded poems in the world. Oh, for a modern James Whitcomb Riley, the editor sighs within. Farmyard philosophy and foolishness made this the barbershop magazine of its day.
59208-mound-state-monument-moundville-al:
Mound State Monument is a guide to the mound site at Moundville, in Alabama. It is Museum Paper 20, in a made new form from the state museum of that land. A list of marks in time heads the guide. A map of the site and the rules of the park stand near the back.

The old town at the site grew and thrived from the years 1200 to 1400. It stood on the banks of the Warrior River, in the west midst of the state. The town was left bare by the year 1500, by that list. White men set a town named Carthage on the spot in 1897. They soon named it Moundville, for the score of mounds in its bounds. First digs came in 1905 and 1906, by Clarence B Moore. The state bought 175 acres in 1929, with most of the 40 mounds in that span.
59271-betsey-bobbett-a-drama:
Betsey Bobbett is a drama in six acts, drawn from the book My Opinions and Betsey Bobbett's. Marietta Holley wrote it under her famous pen name, Josiah Allen's Wife. She entered it at Washington in 1880. The cast lists Josiah Allen, a farmer, and Samantha, his wife, with their daughter Tirzah Ann and son Thomas Jefferson.

Betsey Bobbett herself is an old maid, with a brother named Shakespeare Bobbett. A doctor, a widow, an elder, a peddler, and the editor of the Jonesville Augur fill out the village. The first scene is a Monday at the Allens': Samantha kneads bread, Tirzah Ann washes, and the elder arranges his sermons in the corner. Samantha, the book's beloved narrator, tells how she married Josiah from pure love,. Holley's dialect humour made her one of America's most read comic writers, and this play brings her folk to the stage.
59664-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang was a famed joke monthly from Robbinsdale, Minnesota. Volume two, number twenty-two, came out in July 1921. Laughs, jests, and rough farm wit fill its pages, under the banner of farmyard fun.

The front pages shout the winter annual to come. Pedigreed Follies of 1921 and 1922 would hold new jokes, jests, and jingles. Captain Billy's Advice to the Lovelorn stood in it, and smokehouse poems besides. Old stage verse is in the list: The Face on the Barroom Floor, The Shooting of Dan McGrew, and Lasca. Four times as large and four times as great, the ad promises, for a few cents by post.
60119-isis-very-much-unveiled-being-the-:
Edmund Garrett wrote Isis Very Much Unveiled, the story of the great Mahatma hoax, told mainly from Theosophical sources and issued from the Westminster Gazette office. Garrett had written on the Afrikander land and on Ibsen before this exposure. His preface sends the reader to Pompeii, where a temple of Isis keeps the secret passage its priests used to make wonders. He aims to show the like passage in the temple of Theosophy.

Part one treats mystification under Madame Blavatsky, the exposure by the Society for Psychical Research, and the years under Annie Besant. A seal, an envelope trick, and copies of Mahatma letters are shown as plates. Parts two and three print answers from officials and members, and a general rejoinder. A postscript treats Judge's Mahatma at bay, with his reply and Garrett's verdict on it.
60902-bellingrath-gardens-mobile-alabama:
A visitor's booklet praises the Bellingrath Gardens near Mobile, Alabama, the charm spot of the deep south. The gate fee stands at two dollars, tax in. The gates stay open the whole year round. The grounds lie on the Isle-Aux-Oies River, some twenty miles from old Mobile and a mile from the bay.

No old gardens these, the booklet owns. The place is young, made by the work and care of Mister and Mrs Bellingrath. Old bushes by the thousand were moved in from gardens of long standing. Azaleas and camellias glow on all sides. Gardenias and sweet olive scent the paths. Roses turn in the shape of a great wheel, and live oaks drip gray moss above.
61362-drug-smuggling-and-taking-in-india:
Drug Smuggling and Taking in India and Burma, published at Calcutta in 1922, is Roy Anderson's account from inside the excise service. Anderson served as superintendent of the Burma Excise Department. His preface, dated March 26, 1921, says no book on the subject existed outside dry official blue books. He writes only what he saw himself.

The chapters open with smugglers, bribery and informers. Two chapters of anecdotes follow, then plain observations. Opium gets three chapters: the drug, the smoking and eating of it, and the habit itself. Morphia, cocaine and hemp drugs close the survey. An appendix adds a history of opium in India and Burma.
61468-memoirs-of-doctor-burney-vol-1-of-:
Memoirs of Doctor Burney, volume one, presents the life of the music historian as arranged by his daughter, Madame d'Arblay. She built the book from his own manuscripts, from family papers, and from her own recollections. It was printed at London in 1832, in three volumes, and a verse from the dedication of Evelina to Doctor Burney stands at the front.

In her preface, called an apology, d'Arblay says the task has seemed a sacred duty since 1814, when her father died. A notice at the front begs all who hold letters of Burney to lend them for a planned fourth volume of correspondence. She writes, she says, as recorder of his worth, with filial love suppressing every fear.
61926-memoirs-of-doctor-burney-vol-2-of-:
Madame d'Arblay shaped the life of her father, Doctor Burney, from his own papers and family notes, in a set dated 1832. The second volume opens with the home circle in a London street and the wide ring of famed friends. Court lists, the Royal Society, and the Literary Club all crowd the roll of his world.

A long tale tells of Omiah, a guest from the South Seas who learned the town and its ways. Burney's son James, a sea captain, was to sail with Captain Cook on his last great voyage. Farewell calls, small talk, and quaint scenes show the warmth of the home Omiah must leave.
62046-memoirs-of-doctor-burney-vol-3-of-:
Madame d'Arblay arranged the Memoirs of Doctor Burney from his manuscripts, family papers, and her own recollections. Edward Moxon published the three volumes at London in 1832. Volume three opens in 1784 with Doctor Johnson near his end. Johnson came home from Lichfield on November 16, too weak to gain by native air.

His note to Burney the next day sends respects to all the dear Burneys, little and great. The family hastens to Bolt Court and finds him cheerful in great pain. D'Arblay copies her diary account of a last, long talk on November 25. Johnson owns his restless nights yet smiles with sad mirth over advice. A daughter's record guards a great friendship's close.
62513-through-british-guiana-to-the-summ:
Through British Guiana to the Summit of Roraima, by Mrs Cecil Clementi, was printed in New York by Dutton, with fourteen plates and a map. A view of Kaietuk Fall stands at the front. Clementi traveled the rivers of the colony to the great table mountain.

Chapters open on the Demerara River, then the Essequibo and the Potaro district. The Potaro Gorge and Kaietuk, Mother of Mists, follow. The ascent to the highland savannahs and a corner of Brazil fill the mid part. The Venezuelan approach and Roraima, Father of Streams, stand near the close, then the return journey. Clementi calls the coast a mournful picture of mud flats fringed with courida and mangrove. Travel readers get a rare climb tale from South America wild interior.
63163-studies-in-the-wagnerian-drama:
Studies in the Wagnerian Drama is a book of music criticism by Henry Edward Krehbiel, published in 1891. Krehbiel was the leading American music critic of his day. The book examines Wagner's music dramas with printed musical examples throughout. In this text the examples can be heard in the electronic edition, the transcriber notes.

The scores are also given as images for readers who want the notes themselves. Some scores differ slightly from the first printing, where the music transcriber corrected mistakes or filled out parts. Krehbiel explains Wagner's methods, motives, and orchestra for American audiences then new to the Bayreuth works. The book helped fix Wagner's place in American concert life.
63188-the-critic-and-the-drama:
The Critic and the Drama is a book of theatre essays by George Jean Nathan, published by Knopf in 1922 and dedicated to Edward Gordon Craig. Its six chapters treat aesthetic jurisprudence, drama as an art, the place of the theatre, the place of acting, and dramatic criticism in general and in America.

Nathan opens with a confession about his trade. Criticism, he argues, is founded on vanity: every critic shows off himself at the expense of the artist he judges. The modest critics merely try to hide that egotism and become doubly absurd; the great ones admit it and make no senseless effort at concealment. The first essay then defines art as a reaching out into the ugliness of the world for vagrant beauty, with criticism as its dream book. The voice throughout is aphoristic, combative and pleased with itself, exactly as the theory demands.
63681-tama:
Tama is a novel by Onoto Watanna, printed by Harper and Brothers in 1910 with plates by Genjiro Kataoka. Watanna's earlier books include A Japanese Nightingale, The Wooing of Wistaria, and The Heart of Hyacinth. A plate in this volume shows the fox-woman among the lotus.

The story is set in Japan, where, as the opening tells, all the people had talked of but one event for days. Small boys astride bamboo poles, kitchen maids, beggars of the street, and the highest in the land share the stir. Tama stands at the centre of that talk. The novel mixes romance with the fox lore of Japan, the fox-woman of its plate hinting at the spell that hangs over the heroine. It is a period piece of the West's taste for Japanese tales, told by its best-known practitioner of the day.
63873-camping-in-the-winter-woods-advent:
Camping in the Winter Woods, a boys' adventure novel by Elmer Russell Gregor, was published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1912. Gregor dedicates the book to his nephew, Charles Russell Gregor, a lad with the ear-marks of a true woodsman. The story follows two boys, Edward Williams and George Rand, who step off a train at a log station in the pine woods of northern Maine.

Twenty five chapters carry them through a winter of hunting, trapping, and camp life. They hunt deer, visit beaver dams, fish through the ice, and face a bull moose, a bear, and a forest fire. They spend Christmas at the cabin and ride logs down the stream before they are called home. The book teaches woodcraft through story, the way boys' outdoor novels of its day often did.
64836-jane-seton-or-the-king-s-advocate-:
James Grant wrote this Scottish historical romance, in a new edition from Routledge in London in 1865. Grant had written 'The Romance of War' and 'The Aide-de-Camp' before it. The king's advocate of the subtitle serves James the Fifth of Scotland, in whose reign the romance is laid.

James was far in advance of the age in which he lived, Grant's preface argues. He joined his forefathers' valour and love of Scotland to elegant taste, the preface goes on. His patronage of science and commerce and his love of romantic adventure made him the idol of the people, while his nobles, the preface warns, stood apart.
65620-a-cruel-enigma:
Paul Bourget wrote a French tale put into English by Julian Cray, printed at London in 1887 from the eighteenth French printing. A long first word paints Bourget himself. He is praised as a poet, a keen critic, and a teller of tales with a wide hold on young French writers.

His gift, the writer holds, is the study of the hidden moves of the mind. He reads the play of motives and shades of feeling with rare tact. His clear style sends those finds to the reader whole. Bourget had made himself at home in London, Florence, Paris and Morocco alike, and his tales probe the self watching age he lived in.
66639-the-world-of-flying-saucers-a-scie:
The World of Flying Saucers, a scientific examination of a major myth of the space age, was written by Donald Menzel and Lyle Boyd. Doubleday published it at Garden City, New York, in 1963. Menzel was a Harvard astronomer. The book is dedicated to Fred Whipple, whose work on meteors, the authors note, furnished more than its share of saucer reports.

Chapter one surveys saucer reports, the Air Force's role, and the scientist's view of evidence. Chapter two retells the Arnold sighting of nine disks and the Maury Island fragments. Later chapters sort air borne objects from balloons to bubbles, and take up the Mantell tragedy, in which a pilot died chasing a light. Menzel argues that mirages, planets, and balloons explain the famed cases. The book is a leading work of calm doubt from the height of the saucer craze.
67148-a-dramatization-of-longfellow-s-hi:
A Dramatization of Longfellow Hiawatha, by De Vine, turns the poem into a play. De Vine entered it for rights in 1895 in the Library of Congress. Rights were also held in Britain, France, Germany, and more lands listed. Six acts present the customs of the native North American Indian in spectacle.

Gitche Manitou descends in act one and bids the tribes cease warfare forever. He fashions a peace pipe, sets the forest afire, and vanishes in smoke. Act two shows Hiawatha childhood, with Nokomis swinging the cradle to a lullaby. Wooings, wedding feasts, dances, and death scenes follow the poem closely in words. Instruction on Indian life is the drama stated public aim.
67680-cutie-a-warm-mamma:
Ben Hecht and Maxwell Bodenheim wrote Cutie, a warm mamma, published by Boar's Head Books in New York in 1952. The pair had earlier produced a tale of Lesbia Lefkovitz, the studio siren. Cutie is written in cantos of brash comic verse, and it opens by introducing the alligator's tonsils.

Cutie herself is a shapely young woman of twenty-one summers, with bobbed hair like a bunch of yellow grapes. The poets claim that one look at her left men kissing their wives with faraway eyes. She burned her wings off every night, they say, and grew them on again every morning. In the second canto she meets Herman Pupick, one of triplets, on her twenty-first birthday. The book is a knowing, slangy burlesque in the manner of the Chicago wits.
6843-tecumseh-a-drama:
Charles Mair's drama Tecumseh opens with a speech to the Osages, recalling how white men first came hungry, feeble, with no place to spread blankets or kindle fires. Native fathers, the speech says, shared freely whatever the Great Spirit gave his red children. That memory frames the tragedy that follows.

Tecumseh, chief of the Shawnees, his brother the Prophet, Tarhay in love with Iena, and chiefs of Wyandot, Miami, Delaware, Kickapoo, and Dakota peoples fill the cast, with warriors, runners, and wives. Mair writes with a Canadian patriot's fire. Tecumseh is a bold, historic drama of a great Native leader's stand.
69095-the-greek-theater-and-its-drama:
The Greek Theater and Its Drama, by Roy Flickinger of Northwestern University, was published by the University of Chicago Press in 1918. A view of the Theater of Dionysus at Athens fronts the book. That view is taken from the Acropolis, looking down on the ruins. Flickinger held the chair of Greek and Latin at his university.

His study treats the building, the stage, and the plays of old Greece. Masks, chorus, and the great festivals stand behind the drama he traces. Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes fill the stage of his account. The book was made for students and for the general reader alike. Photographs and plans ground the text in stone and dust. It remains a clear doorway into the birth of western theatre.
69140-remember-me-kama:
Walter Kubilius opens on a standoff in Remember Me, Kama!, from Astonishing Stories in October 1942. Old Cobber sits in his tankbox on a poison-aired planet, guns trained on the crew clearing ammonia snow from the rocket's jets. Wilson warns him he is outnumbered thirty to one.

Cobber answers that he will blow up the ship, and opens a dinatro bomb as the men scatter for the cliffs. He counts the seconds down and whispers the title words to himself. Beyond the standoff waits the Great Kama, and the charred bodies of the Kamae, and a wrong to be answered.
69208-sir-lawrence-alma-tadema:
Sir Lawrence Alma Tadema is a small life and work book by Helen Zimmern. The book stands in a miniature set of painter lives for home shelves. It came out in London in the year nineteen hundred and two. A front plate shows a child scene with a line on heaven in a child.

Parts treat the life, the work, and the craft of the man in turn. Lists name his chief pictures and portraits, with the homes that hold them. He was born in Holland in eighteen thirty six and made England his home. Marble halls, Roman feasts, and Greek song form his famed world of paint. Photo plates in the book show that bright calm world at small scale.
69218-the-worship-of-the-golden-calf-a-s:
The Worship of the Golden Calf is a novel of wage slavery by Charles Sheldon French. The author published it himself at Dalton, Massachusetts, in 1908. A note updates a point of law in the text. Ten thousand dollars may now be had for a life lost by a railway's fault. The tale opens in the Berkshire hills in early spring. John Wycliff, a farm labourer, waits for his month's pay.

Wycliff has lost one eye and bears a bent nose. Indians and a cattle stampede left those marks. He has been editor, cowboy, and gold miner. Once he held part of a gold mine. That mine is now thought worthless. He is a common labourer again at the start. French writes from inside the mill country. The golden calf of the title is money itself.
70624-sanitation-in-panama:
Sanitation in Panama, by William Crawford Gorgas, chief sanitary officer of the Panama Canal and surgeon general of the army. D Appleton and Company published the book at New York and London in 1915. A concreted ditch at Ancon serves as frontispiece.

Early chapters give yellow fever and the discoveries of its transmission, then the experiments of the Reed Board at Havana. Gorgas follows the sanitary work at Havana before his own appointment to the Isthmus. The Panama chapters cover yellow-fever work, the sanitary inspectors, the hospitals at Ancon, malaria, the leper colony, quarantine, and measures against bubonic plague.
70937-the-photodrama:
Henry Albert Phillips wrote a practical treatise on the photodrama, printed at Larchmont, New York, in 1914 in a second edition. Phillips had served on the staff of Pathe Freres. The book stands in the Authors' Hand Book series. It is given to all literary workers who strive to elevate and dignify the photodrama.

Part one sets out the principles: a new medium of artistic expression. The premise of all art, the battle of new standards, and the drama of the eye head the first chapter. All the world's the stage, and a field without limitations, it cries. How photodrama differs from stage drama follows. Title, synopsis, cast of characters, scenario, the scene, and the setting are laid out. A complete photoplay and a glossary close a pioneer manual for film writers.
71045-the-interpretation-of-dreams-and-m:
The Interpretation of Dreams and Moles is a penny chapbook on fortune telling, printed by Marshall at Newcastle upon Tyne. The title page adds other curious matters relating to love and courtship. The printer's shop also sold songs, ballads, tales, and histories. The contents list ten parts, from the views of sages on dreams to the lines of the hand.

The opening argues that dreams carry meaning, as wise men of all ages held. While the body sleeps, the soul speaks with spirits and learns things to come. Scripture dreams of Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar are cited as proof. Plain rules follow: to dream of flying promises hasty news. To dream of swimming with pleasure means beating a hard matter in hand. Other parts read moles, teach how to choose a spouse, and tell fortune by the palm.
71881-the-magazine-of-history-with-notes:
The Magazine of History with Notes and Queries, volume 1, number 5, was dated May 1905 in New York. William Abbatt published the monthly at five dollars a year, or fifty cents a number. A front plate from a Birch painting shows the moonlight battle of the Bon Homme Richard and the Serapis on September 23. Contents mix essays, poems, and original documents.

Warren Upham writes on the discovery of the Mississippi River, and Walter Fleming on Confederate finance in Alabama. Other pieces treat freedom of the press, antiquities of the Southwest, and John Paul Jones' fellow officers. Letters from Poe, Lincoln, and Washington are printed as documents. Book notices and society news close a rich number for American history buffs.
72708-paddle-and-portage-from-moosehead-:
Paddle and Portage is a canoeing narrative by Thomas Sedgwick Steele. Estes and Lauriat of Boston published it in 1882. More than sixty illustrations, and a large map, accompany the text. The map charts the canoe courses of northern Maine for its readers.

The journey runs from Moosehead Lake to the Aroostook River in Maine. Steele dedicates the book to Lyman Goff, his companion on the tour. They had shared its pleasures, dangers, discomforts, and successes together. The contents open with the start, the guides, and the outfit. A flimsy wharf and the railroading of the old days give local colour. The first carries bring the commencement of fun, in the chapter's phrase. A first night in the wilds closes the opening movement. Pine Stream Falls and Chesuncook Lake wait in the chapters that follow.
72797-ten-years-in-burma:
Julius Smith recorded ten years of missionary life in Burma here. Jennings and Pye printed the account at Cincinnati in 1902. The preface says America now holds large tropical lands of its own. Burma matches the Philippine Islands in climate, he notes there.

Burmese and Tagal races hold great likeness, the preface adds. No printed account of the Methodist mission stood for twenty two years. Smith gives that mission record permanent form in this volume here. Races, social life, and government of Burma fill its pages too. Eaton and Mains shared the New York side of the book trade for the volume.
73184-four-years-in-upper-burma:
Four Years in Upper Burma, by Winston, was published in London in 1892. A motto from a poem urges spreading mercy where Britain power is felt. Sacred buildings of the Buddhists form a front picture. A preface disclaims any first intention of writing a book.

All he purposed, Winston says, was to prepare a short report of work done. The interesting material at hand proved too abundant to compress within his intended limits. The need for better knowledge, among English people generally, of the distant dependencies of the British Empire is undeniable, he argues. If they are to govern the many races placed in their hands at all intelligently, they must know them. He tells of a member of Parliament who did not know Burma from Bermuda. Readers get a mission report grown into a country survey.
74147-the-black-drama:
The Black Drama is a weird tale by Field, printed in Weird Tales across June, July, and August 1938. A headnote promises a strange story about the eerie personality known as Varduk, who claimed descent from Lord Byron, and the hideous doom that stalked in his wake. A Byron line from Manfred stands at the head.

The foreword is signed by Gilbert Connatt, an actor, at New York on August 1, 1938. Unlike most actors, he writes, he does not think his memoirs worth public attention; he seals this record for his descendants. Three witnesses sign that his statement is true in substance. The tale then opens below Times Square, where Connatt has fifteen cents and orders a hamburger.
74314-the-sanskrit-drama:
Sanskrit Drama, in its origin, development, theory, and practice, is a scholarly work by Berriedale Keith. Oxford University Press published the book for its author in London. Keith was regius professor of Sanskrit and comparative philology at the University of Edinburgh. He was of the Inner Temple and of the Scottish Bar as well in his titles.

Contents divide the work into parts, of which the first treats the origin of the drama. Dramatic elements in Vedic literature open the survey in the first chapter. The Indian tradition of the origin of the drama, the dialogues of the Veda, and dramatic elements in Vedic ritual fill that chapter.  Keith history remains a standard account of how India made a theatre out of rite and epic, written with a lawyers care for the evidence of each claim.
74773-the-freed-boy-in-alabama:
Anne M Mitchell wrote The Freed Boy in Alabama. The Presbyterian Board of Publication issued it at Philadelphia. Copyright ran in 1869 under Wm L Hildeburn. Mitchell had written Martha's Gift before this. A Bible line heads the book in brief. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.

A front plate shows a man hailing the boy. Say, Boy, do you want to hire out, it asks. Chapter One opens on an April day. The South's spring stands warm and lovely there. Grass springs and buds burst all around, she writes. Bryant's spring verses head the chapter. Tender leaves invite a caressing touch, she says. Restless longing fills such a day, she adds. A freed boy's path through work and faith in the new South fills this Sunday school tale of Reconstruction times.
77420-a-true-relation-of-the-travels-and:
Mathew Dudgeon wrote his own account of his travels and perilous adventures, printed for the first time in London in 1894. Dudgeon came from a family of position near Portsmouth, where tales from old sailors gave him a taste for the sea. As a younger son, he had to seek a trade.

His uncle, a Turkey merchant in London, took him into the office at the Barbican to learn the business. Dudgeon later made many voyages for his uncle to the East and West Indies, and twice suffered shipwreck. He won his uncle's trust, married, and inherited a large part of the property and the firm. The title promises the heart of the tale: his capture, his long slavery in Algiers, and the means of his delivery. Readers get a seaman's own record of trade, wreck, and captivity.
78038-sodoma:
The Contessa Priuli-Bon wrote a life of the painter Sodoma for the Great Masters in Painting and Sculpture series. Williamson edited the series, and George Bell and Sons issued the book at London in 1900. Seven chapters trace the artist from his origin and early life to Monte Oliveto, to Rome, and to success at Siena. An unknown stretch and a return to Siena come before his later years.

A final chapter weighs his general character as man and painter. Then come a catalogue of the works, placed by country and by the towns and galleries that hold them, a dated list of the works, papers, and an index. Plates show the Saint Sebastian, the Deposition, and the fresco work at the Villa Farnesina in Rome.
7834-wagner-s-tristan-und-isolde-an-essa:
George Ainslie Hight's essay on Wagner's Tristan und Isolde opens with Whitman's lines on passing visions, night, and a victorious song that floods earth and heaven. The preface says the pages hold little new for Wagner experts, but aim at beginners who want to know what Wagner sought.

No English book, Hight argues, yet tells a newcomer how Wagner's dramas differ from earlier opera, so an introduction is needed first. Through Tristan's love, night, and death song, the essay guides fresh listeners into music drama, where words, orchestra, and myth fuse into one work.
9232-passages-from-a-relinquished-work-f:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote these passages for Mosses from an Old Manse, from a work he gave up. The narrator, raised by a village parson who prayed daily and whipped freely, contrasts his own course with the parson's three sons. They grew respectable: one a minister, one a doctor, one a shoe merchant. He, with better prospects, ran another road.

Yet he doubts whether their success would have contented him, once his own misfortunes taught him otherwise. Hawthorne's fragment reads as a confession in embryo. It remains a fascinating glimpse of a novel that never was, and of its author's early mind.
9378-the-lone-wolf-a-melodrama:
Louis Joseph Vance wrote this Paris melodrama in 1914, opening at Troyon's restaurant. Bourke, proud to be Irish, joked that even if you knew Paris you had to lose your way to find Troyon's, tucked in a jungle of side streets near St. Germain. Its hero, the Lone Wolf, moves through stratagems, flights, and unmaskings.

Chapters run from return and anticlimax to war, apostasy, and daybreak, with Madame Omber and a rendezvous along the way. Vance keeps the pace breathless and the city vivid. The novel remains a stylish thriller of pre-war Paris, full of rogues and romance.
a-new-england-girlhood-outlined-from-mem:
Lucy Larcom outlines her own girlhood in Beverly, Massachusetts, from memory, writing for the young at the suggestion of friends, as her preface says. She dedicates the sketch to her girlfriends in general. The contents begin Up and Down the Lane, then Schoolroom and Meeting-House, the Hymn-Book, and Naughty Children and Fairy Tales.

Later chapters cover beginning to work, mill-girls' magazines, and reading and studying, and close with a move from the Merrimack to the Mississippi. Larcom had worked in the Lowell mills as a girl, and she writes of books, hymns, and sea air with equal love. Her memoir remains a gentle, exact picture of a New England childhood.
an-account-of-the-customs-and-manners-of: Antoine Simon Maillard records the customs and manners of the Micmakis and Maricheets, nations then dependent on the government of Cape Breton. Published in London, the account describes their daily life, beliefs, and dealings with Europeans. It remains an early, if colonial in outlook, source on the Indigenous peoples of the Atlantic coast.
britannica-1911-abbott-emma: Emma Abbott is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names an American singer, born at Chicago in 1849, who studied in Milan and Paris. A fine soprano voice carried her to opera in London under Colonel Mapleson at Covent Garden, and to leading concerts. She then formed an opera company under her own name and toured the United States widely, winning a great reputation there. She married E J Wetherell in 1873. She died at Salt Lake City in January 1891, the entry closes.
britannica-1911-aceldama:
Aceldama, according to the Acts of the Apostles, means the field of blood, the name given to the field bought with the money Judas Iscariot received for betraying Jesus. Matthew's gospel tells the purchase differently: Judas threw the money down in the Temple, and the priests used it to buy the potter's field for burying strangers. The entry weighs manuscript spellings and even a rival reading, field of sleep, meaning a cemetery.

Tradition fixed a site south of Jerusalem, on the slope of the Hill of Evil Counsel. Christian pilgrims were buried there from the sixth century into the seventeenth, especially in crusading times. A very ancient charnel-house, partly cut in rock, stands nearby.
britannica-1911-alma:
