Alma is a river in the south-west of the Crimea that enters the Black Sea north of Sevastopol. Its name is famous for a battle fought on its banks on 20 September 1854, during the Crimean War. Russian forces under Prince Menshikov held a steep ridge along the south bank, barring the road to Sevastopol against allied armies approaching across an open plain from the north.

British troops under Lord Raglan and French under Marshal St Arnaud shared the allied command, with Turkish forces alongside the French. The French scaled the cliffs on the seaward flank with little early opposition, while the British deployed and assaulted the Russian front directly. Menshikov fed his reserves in piecemeal and finally drew his army off southwards. The entry gives detailed force and casualty figures from named authorities, recording a costly allied victory.
britannica-1911-bema:
Bema, a Greek word, in church building names the half-round recess, or exedra, of a basilica. Judges sat there in Roman times, and in later days the altar took that place. A half dome usually roofs it, priests’ seats line the wall, and the bishop’s seat stands in the middle, reached by steps and fenced by a rail.

In Greece the word covered any raised platform. At Athens it was the stone stand, ten or eleven feet high on the Pnyx, from which speakers addressed the citizens’ assembly. Law-court speakers used one too, and another bema held the urns for the bronze disks by which judges cast their votes in the late fourth century.
britannica-1911-bilma:
Bilma, also called Kawar, is an oasis in the heart of the Sahara desert. The oasis runs some 60 miles long by ten miles broad. Its people are Tibbu and Kanuri. The chief settlement, Bilma or Garu, lies in the southern part. It stands 800 miles due south of Tripoli, and about 350 miles north of Lake Chad's north-west corner. Salt lakes near the town anchor its whole economy.

When the lake water dries, it leaves large amounts of very pure, fine salt. That salt feeds an extensive trade with central African countries, the 1911 Britannica entry says. North of Bilma stands Dirki, said to date from the 11th century. South of the oasis begins the Sahara's dreariest stretch, fifteen days without plant life. Day heat rarely fell below 113 degrees Fahrenheit on Nachtigal's 1870 visit. A French force occupied the town in 1906.
britannica-1911-birmingham-alabama:
Birmingham is a city in Jefferson County, Alabama, seat of the county. It stands in the north-central part of the state, 96 miles north-west of Montgomery. Its height is 600 feet, in Jones Valley between two mountain ridges. Nine railway lines serve the city in the 1911 Britannica entry. Growth was explosive: 26,178 people in 1890, 38,415 in 1900, and 132,685 in 1910. Sixteen public parks dot the city, with East Lake and Capitol parks praised.

The city is a child of the South's industrial turn after the Civil War. In 1870 its site was a cotton field where two railways crossed. A land company founded Birmingham in 1871. Within four months 1,200 people lived there, and 2,500 by 1873. Iron and steel anchor its economy in the entry's account. Cotton-seed oil, yarn, furniture, machinery, and lumber all add to its output.
britannica-1911-boma:
Boma, properly Mboma, is a port on the north bank of the Congo River about 60 miles from its mouth, and the administrative capital of Belgian Congo when the entry was written. About 5000 people lived there. European traders had kept stations at Boma since the 1500s and 1600s.

It became the main trading post for the lower Congo and a well-known slave market. Dutch merchants ran most of the trade, with British, French, and Portuguese houses beside them. No European power truly ruled there, though Portugal now and then claimed it. In 1884 the people of Boma granted a protectorate over their country to the International Association of the Congo, the seed of the Congo Free State.
britannica-1911-charles-ii-duke-of-parma:
Charles II of Parma, born Charles Louis de Bourbon (1799-1883), is the subject of an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which gives a sharp view of his rule. He succeeded his mother as duke of Lucca in 1824. He cut costs, added schools, and in 1832 became a Protestant, reacting against the bigotry around his upbringing.

The entry says his early liberal leanings, shown by shelter given to Modenese refugees, soon gave way to folly and waste that made him a laughing stock. He returned to the Catholic Church in 1842 and made an English groom his prime minister. In 1847 he sold his interest in Lucca, then succeeded to Parma, where his rule brought ruinous finance and disorder.
britannica-1911-clough-anne-jemima:
Clough, Anne Jemima (1820–1892) was an English educationalist, born at Liverpool on 20 January 1820, daughter of a cotton merchant and sister of the poet Arthur Hugh Clough. Taken to Charleston, South Carolina, at two, she returned to England in 1836 wanting to write, yet spent her life mostly in teaching. Her father's business failure led her to open a school in 1841, carried on until 1846. A second small school at Ambleside followed from 1852.

Keenly interested in women's education, she befriended Emily Davies, Madame Bodichon and Miss Buss, and helped found the North of England council for women's higher education. When a house for women students at Cambridge was decided on, she was chosen as its first principal. That hostel, begun in Regent Street in 1871 with five students, led to Newnham Hall in 1875 and Newnham College in 1880. She died at Cambridge on 27 February 1892.
britannica-1911-cocoma:
Cocoma, also called Cucamas, are a tribe of South American Indians living on two rivers in Peru. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives them a short entry written in the terms of its day. Their home lay on the Marañon and the lower Huallaga. When Jesuit missionaries first visited them in 1681, the Cocoma had a custom that shocked their guests. They ate their dead and ground the bones to a powder, which was mixed with a fermented liquor and drunk.

Questioned by the Jesuits, they answered that it was better to be inside a friend than to be swallowed by the cold earth. The entry calls them a provident, hard working people, partly Christianized, and bolder than most of the civilized Indians of the region. Their languages show a kinship with the Tupi Guarani stock, a point that places them among the wider peoples of the Amazon basin.
britannica-1911-coma:
Coma in the care of the sick is set out as a deep loss of sense in a 1911 Britannica health entry. The word comes from a Greek word for deep sleep. In care use it means more than sleep, the text warns. The sick man cannot be waked from the state at all. Light forms let him stir for a bit, then sink back at once.

Head wounds, strong drink, and brain bleed can bring the state on at a stroke. Ills such as sugar sickness and kidney failure bring it on by slow steps. Breath paces shift in a set wave as death nears in some cases. That wave is named for Cheyne and Stokes in the text. Depth of the state is read by how the eyes and limbs fail to react to touch.
britannica-1911-comma:
Comma comes from a Greek word for a thing cut off, from a verb that means to strike. In Greek rhetoric it first named a short clause, less than a colon. From that it came to name the mark (,) in punctuation. The mark shows the least break in the build of a sentence. It is also used to part numbers, signs in sums, and the like.

Pairs of commas, the first turned and the last upright, form what are called inverted commas. They stand at the start and end of words that are quoted. They also mark a word used in a trade or set sense. Single commas serve for quotes inside quotes. The word is also used for things shaped like a comma. One case is the comma-bacillus, the agent held to cause cholera.
britannica-1911-crema:
Crema is a town of Lombardy in Italy, in the province of Cremona. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its churches and past. It stands on the right bank of the Serio River. Rich farm land spreads around it on every side. Its town count in 1901 was about eight thousand.

The cathedral shows a fine Lombard Gothic front from the late 1300s. A clock tower across the square dates from Venetian rule. The town castle, once among the strongest in Italy, was torn down in 1809. Crema first stood out in the tenth century as a chief place. Barbarossa sacked it in 1160, and it was rebuilt in 1185. Venice held the town from 1449 for more than three centuries.
britannica-1911-empyema: Empyema is a medical term in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, and the hosted entry is a single short definition rather than a full article. Built from Greek words for “within” and “pus,” it names a gathering of purulent fluid inside the cavity of the pleura. The pleura is the membrane around the lungs, and the entry adds nothing about causes, signs, or treatment. It simply fixes the term's meaning and points the reader onward to the article on the lung and its surgery for the fuller account.
britannica-1911-enigma:
Enigma is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a riddle or puzzle form. The word comes from Greek. An enigma hides its answer behind word pictures, in verse or in prose. The riddle of the Sphinx is given as the famed case.

The article sketches the long life of the form. Riddle making was a loved pastime in Greece, with prizes given at feasts. In France of the 1600s the craft came into high fashion. Great writers there did not think it beneath them to make such puzzles. A printed set of the riddles of the time came out in 1646. The word also names, in looser use, any thing hard to grasp.
britannica-1911-fama:
Fama, the shaped form of rumour in old myth, is weighed in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Homer's Ossa acts as the swift voice of Zeus in the Iliad. She spreads news as fast as a fire takes hold. Homer does not shape Pheme as a god in the same way. For him she is more a sign drawn from men's words.

Hesiod calls Pheme a goddess in his Works and Days. Sophocles names her the deathless child of golden Hope. Athens kept a temple of Pheme, the entry records. Smyrna kept a shrine of the Cledones, sounds read as omens. Rome gave Fama no cult, holding her a shape of verse. Virgil and Ovid left the famed word pictures of her.
britannica-1911-lazarus-emma:
Emma Lazarus, who lived from 1849 to 1887, was an American Jewish poet. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces her growth as a writer. Born in New York, she wrote verse from her teens. Her first book held poems and translations made before age eighteen.

Emerson guided her early work and wrote to her for years. She printed poems in magazines and a prose tale based on Goethe. Her renderings of Heine poems won wide praise in 1881. Attacks on Jews in Russia then turned her verse to her own people. Poems and plays in Songs of a Semite called Jews to unity and action. She gave her last years to that cause and died in 1887.
britannica-1911-llama:
Llama is an animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the larger of the two tame members of the camel tribe native to South America. The llama is a tame offshoot of the wild guanaco and has been bred as a beast of burden. It is found chiefly in southern Peru, grows larger than the guanaco, and is most often white, or white marked with brown or black.

The article quotes at length an account by Augustin de Zarate from 1544. Zarate tells how the great sheep of Peru carry loads of a hundred pounds or more and walk four or five leagues a day. He praises their fine wool, their rich flesh, and how little they cost to keep, since a handful of maize feeds them. The spitting habit, the article adds, runs through the whole group.
britannica-1911-massa-marittima:
Massa Marittima is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a town in Tuscany, Italy. It stands 1,444 feet above the sea in Grosseto province. The town count for 1901 is 9,219 folk. The wider commune held 17,519 folk at that same count.

Its great church dates from the thirteenth century and holds fine old work. A font from 1267 and a shrine case from 1324 are named. The walled town hall of the same age is called a fine sight. Springs and mines of iron, mercury, and copper lie in its lands. Foundries, iron works, and olive oil mills give it work. At Follonica the iron ore of Elba is smelted in its furnaces.
britannica-1911-melodrama:
Melodrama is a coined word for a kind of stage play with music. The 1911 Britannica entry builds the word from Greek parts for music and action. In its strict sense it names drama where music backs speech. No singing took place in that early form of the art. Speech and act ran on while music played beneath them both.

Rousseau's Pygmalion of 1775 is oft named the first such work. From that seed grew the romantic plays of strong, wild incident. Those plays lean on stock types in place of true character. The villain, the wronged hero, and the chased heroine fill their casts. Music shrank in time to a cue for big scenes and entrances.
britannica-1911-oshima: Oshima is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a group of small islands of Japan. The group of three lies south of Kiushiu island. Their names from west to east are Kuroshima, Iwo-shima, and Takashima. Kuro-shima rises to 2,475 feet above the sea. Iwo-shima has a live volcano 2,480 feet high. More isles in Japan share this name, the entry warns. Oshima means big island in that land.
britannica-1911-ottava-rima:
Ottava Rima is a verse article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Italian stanza form. The stanza has eight iambic lines with three rhymes, always arranged in one fixed pattern. It is an Italian invention, and the earliest examples come from the fourteenth century. Those epics gave the form its classic character.

The article traces the measure through Italy and into England. Boiardo used it for the Orlando Innamorato, and Pulci gave it its comic tone. Ariosto and Tasso wielded it with great charm. The turn came in 1817 with Frere's Whistlecraft, which caught the movement of the Italian measure. Byron answered with Beppo and then wrote Don Juan. The article also notes Shelley's use of it for translations of Homer in 1820.
britannica-1911-pagan-burma:
Pagan is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pagan was a town and former capital in Upper Burma. King Pyinbya founded it in 847, and it stayed the capital until 1298. By the time of the article it had shrunk to a mere village.

What makes Pagan notable is its field of temples. Hundreds of pagodas stand around it in many stages of decay. Most were built by King Anawra-hta, who brought the Buddhist faith to Upper Burma. He carried off people from Thaton to build the temples on Thaton models. The entry notes that Pagan stayed a place of pilgrimage. A museum had been built there to show finds from the area.
britannica-1911-panderma: Panderma, called Panormus in Greek, is a town of Asia Minor given a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the south shore of the Sea of Marmora. The site lies near the ruins of ancient Cyzicus. A carriage road links the town with Balikisri inland. Its people number about ten thousand, of whom seven thousand are given as Moslems. The town trades in grain, cotton, opium, valonia, and boracite.
britannica-1911-parma:
Parma, a fine city of north Italy, is surveyed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on its own stream, a feeder of the Po River. Bologna lies fifty-five miles to the south-east by rail from it. In 1906 its folk came to over forty-eight thousand in count. The Lombard plain spreads rich and flat around the city walls.

Old walls and bastions ring the town in a wide loop. The Via Aemilia runs east to west through its heart today. That Roman road once tied Parma to Rimini and Piacenza. At the centre the road spreads into the Piazza Garibaldi. Town and state palaces of 1627 face that great square. Its cathedral rose in the years after the first millennium.
britannica-1911-puma:
Puma is an animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about one of the largest cats of the New World. The name came into print through early Spanish writers on South America. French writers call the beast the cougar, and hunters in the United States call it the panther.

The article gives the cat's build in detail. It runs about forty inches from nose to tail root, with a long tail past half that span. The head is small, the ears large and round, and there is no mane. The coat is a tawny yellow brown above and a dull white below. Cubs are born spotted, but the marks fade as they grow. The range runs from Canada clear down to Patagonia. The text notes its climbing skill and its wasteful killing of farm stock.
britannica-1911-raba-ben-joseph-ben-hama: Raba ben Joseph ben Hama (about 280 to 352) was a Babylonian rabbi, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is closely linked in his studies with Abaye, head of the academy at Pumbeditha. Raba founded a new school at Mahuza, which while he lived became the only academy in Babylonia. The entry says the growth of Talmudic law owed much to this rabbi, whose sway was supreme. His friendship with King Shapur II won a softening of harsh laws laid on Persia's Jews.
britannica-1911-rovuma:
Rovuma is the name of a river in East Africa, treated here in a 1911 Britannica article on its course and banks. For much of its length the river formed the line between German and Portuguese land. Its main stream rises on a high plateau east of Lake Nyasa and flows first west, then south and east toward the sea.

The lower river forms where two branches meet, the longer one being the Lujenda from the south-west. That branch starts near Lake Chilwa, passes through Lake Chiuta and Lake Amaramba, and grows wide with wooded isles. The main river is shallow, can be crossed on foot in the dry months, and is about a mile wide at its mouth.
britannica-1911-sakura-jima: Sakura-Jima is a Japanese island, oval in shape, seven miles by five. It lies in the north part of the Bay of Kagoshima. The island has a volcano 3,743 feet high, with a burst on record in 1779. It is famed for its hot springs, its oranges, and its giant radishes. Those radishes, called daikon, can at times weigh as much as 70 pounds, as the short article notes.
britannica-1911-sulitelma: Sulitelma is a mountain on the border between Norway and Sweden, noted in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It forms a point of the main range of the Scandinavian peninsula. The mass holds three peaks and a snow field. Many ice streams flow down from that snow. They feed two Swedish rivers that run to the south east. Lakes and fjord foothills lie to the west. A mining town at its base links by boat and light rail to the sea.
britannica-1911-tacoma:
Tacoma is the subject of a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tacoma is a city in Pierce County in Washington. It stands on Commencement Bay of Puget Sound, at the mouth of the Puyallup River. It lies southwest of Seattle. By 1910 its people numbered near eighty four thousand, a sharp rise in ten years.

The article lists rail lines and ship lines that serve the city. Ships sail to Alaska, Japan, China, and ports in Britain. The city has twenty five miles of waterfront on a fine harbour. From the shore the land slopes up to a high plateau with wide views. Schools include Whitworth College and the University of Puget Sound. The text also notes a Carnegie library, a museum, and seven public parks.
britannica-1911-trachoma: Trachoma is a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a disease of the eye. It is a lasting, wasting swelling of the inner lid, also called granular conjunctivitis. A second name for it is Egyptian ophthalmia. The disease spreads from person to person and goes with dirty ways of life. It is common in Egypt and Arabia and in parts of Europe. Its spread had made it a live care at the ports of Britain and America, where newcomers found with it were turned back.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alabama:
Alabama, twenty-second into the Federal Union of America, lies north of the Gulf of Mexico, counting among the Gulf, or South Central, states. Tennessee lies north, Georgia east, the Gulf and Florida south, and Mississippi west. From north to south it measures 336 miles, east to west 148 to 200 miles. Its area is 52,250 square miles, 710 water and 51,540 land.

The state divides roughly into the Tennessee Valley, the mineral region, the cotton belt, and the timber and coast regions. Northern vegetation belongs to the temperate zone, southern to the semi-tropical. Fine hardwood and ordinary timber spread well over the whole state. The principal crop is cotton, yielding 1,249,685 bales in 1905 and giving the state third place in cotton production. The entry then traces Alabama's history and Catholic missions and institutions there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alma:
Alma is a Hebrew word for a young woman, married or not, and so differs from bethulah, a virgin. The interest in the word comes from the famous passage of Isaiah 7:14, 'the Alma shall conceive.' Various opinions are offered about the Alma in this verse is said to be Achaz's wife, the prophetess of Isaiah 8:3, or any young married woman. Such a woman, because of the promised victory of Judah, she could soon call her child Immanuel, God with us. Metaphorically, the Alma could mean the Chosen People.

The last view offered is the Virgin Mother of the Messiah, the reading St. Matthew 1:23 adopts and Christian tradition follows. The distinction matters because bethulah unambiguously means virgin, while alma leaves the question open, and Christian tradition reads the verse through Matthew's Gospel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ama:
Ama, or Amma, is a Semitic term for mother, adopted by Copts and Greeks as an honour title for religious women and ladies of high rank. Coptic inscriptions give it to both categories, and Greeks used it much as Latin used abbatissa, or abbess. Ama, or amula, also names a vessel receiving the people's wine offering for the Holy Sacrifice.

Pope Adrian I, who reigned 772 to 795, presented an ama to St. Adrian's Church. One word thus covers a title of reverence and a liturgical vessel, both rooted in early Christian usage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anathema:
Anathema comes from a Greek word meaning placed on high, suspended, or set aside. It first named offerings hung on temple walls or roofs for all to see. The Old and New Testaments use it in that sense, for Judith's offering, for gifts Antiochus promised the temple, and for the rich gifts adorning the temple in Luke.

Since hateful things were also put on view, such as a criminal's head or spoils, the word came to mean a thing cursed and cut off, matching the Hebrew herem. In church law it grew into the gravest form of excommunication, solemnly pronounced, as against a cleric who stayed incorrigible after deposition and exclusion. Gregory IX later fixed the line between minor and major excommunication, and anathema kept its place as major excommunication with added ceremony. Its formulas still left room for repentance, since the Church seeks the sinner's conversion, not his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-john-:
Blessed John of Parma, Minister General of the Friars Minor from 1247 to 1257, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Parma about 1209, probably of the Buralli family, he died at Camerino in 1289. Taught by an uncle, chaplain of St. Lazarus at Parma, he became a teacher of philosophy and entered the Franciscans, probably in 1233.

Ordained, he taught theology at Bologna and Naples and read the Sentences at Paris, attending Lyons I in 1245. As general he refused to burden friars with new statutes, sent an embassy for Greek reunion that hailed him angel of peace, and resigned in 1257. The entry presents a gentle ruler of a troubled order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burma:
Before British rule, Burma held the kingdoms of Ava and Pegu, and Catholic missions there began slowly. Saint Francis Xavier sought missionaries for Pegu in 1548, but real work waited until 1722, when Innocent XIII sent the Barnabites Sigismond de Calchi and Vittoni. Benedict XIV set the mission on a firm footing in 1741, yet wars killed the last Barnabites left in the country.

Pius VIII and Gregory XVI then handed the mission to new hands, and by 1845 the two kingdoms counted 2,500 Catholics. Britain annexed Pegu in 1852 and later took Ava, so the whole of Burma passed to Great Britain. In 1855 the vicariate stood under the Vicar Apostolic of Siam, with 11 priests and 5,320 Catholics in the two kingdoms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calama:
Calama, likely the Roman name of Suthul in Numidia, besieged by Postumius in 110 B.C., became a municipium under Hadrian and a colony soon after. Vandals took it on reaching Africa in 429, and Count Bonifacius was beaten near it in 431. Inscriptions found at Guelma prove that town the modern heir of Calama, today a district capital in Algeria with 7,300 people and a cattle market.

Four bishops are known: Donatus in 305, Megalius, who consecrated Saint Augustine in 395, Saint Possidius, elected in 397, and Quodvultdeus in 484. Possidius, Augustine's disciple in the monastic life, endured persecution from pagans and Donatists at Calama, later joined Augustine on his deathbed at Hippo, and wrote his master's life and catalogue of works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colima:
This entry describes Colima, a city in Mexico and capital of the state of the same name. It stands on the Colima River at 1,400 feet. Gonzalo de Sandoval founded it in 1522. By 1900 it held 20,698 people. The Diocese of Colima was erected by Leo XIII on 11 December 1881, through the constitution Si principum. Before that, the district had long formed part of the Archdiocese of Guadalajara. Now it stands as a suffragan of Guadalajara.

Its bounds take in the whole State of Colima and the southern part of Jalisco. Its population in 1901 numbered 72,500, many of them Indians. Short and factual, the entry gives a reader the city's founding and its church history. It also gives its scale at the turn of the century, in a single compact sketch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crema:
A diocesan entry sketches Crema, a city of Lombardy between the Adda and Oglio rivers, and its see, suffragan to Milan. Built by refugees fleeing the Lombard invasion, Crema became among the first cities to form a commune. It entered the Lombard League and was destroyed by Frederick Barbarossa, then by Cremona and Lodi.

After rule by the Torriani, Visconti, and Benzoni, it finally passed to the Republic of Venice. Until 1580 Crema belonged to the Diocese of Lodi; then it became a see of its own. Its most noted bishop was the zealous Marcantonio Zolli. The diocese counted 58,000 people, 53 parishes, and 174 secular priests at the time of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dogma:
Dogma is a word with a long career before it reached theology. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry starts with the Greek sense, an opinion, a school's tenet, or a public decree. Scripture uses it for Caesar's edict at the birth of Christ and for ordinances of the Mosaic Law. From these roots the Church shaped its own sense, a truth set forth by divine authority for belief.

The entry then surveys how dogmas are defined, how they grow in the Church's mind, and how they bind the faithful. It draws on the great dogmatic writers, from the fathers to Newman, and it closes with a shelf of handbooks. Readers will find a word history that opens into a full account of Catholic teaching authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-drachma:
The drachma was a Greek silver coin whose name began as a handful of grain. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry derives the word from a Greek verb for gripping, matching the Latin handful. Vigouroux instead traces it to a Persian coin name, daraq-mana, a part of a mina, since the Persian word for degree gives the sense of division. The coin was also called a daric, for Darius Hystaspis first struck it.

Six obols made a drachma, which equaled a quarter of a stater, a hundredth of a mina, and a six-thousandth of a talent. Its exact worth shifted with place and time. The word appears in Christ's parable of a woman holding ten drachmas and losing one, a coin the old Douay version renders as a groat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haceldama:
Haceldama, Aramaic for field of blood, is the people's name for the potter's field bought with Judas's thirty pieces of silver. Matthew tells how Judas threw the money into the temple and hanged himself. The chief priests, refusing blood money for the temple treasury, bought the field as a burial ground for strangers.

Acts tells the same field differently, as ground Judas himself acquired and where he burst asunder. The entry reconciles the two by noting that Peter spoke as an orator recalling a death, while Matthew wrote as a historian tracing prophecy. Pilgrims' tradition kept the place south of Jerusalem in the valley of Hinnom, where crusaders later built a great charnel house and burials continued into the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-bayma:
Joseph Bayma was an Italian Jesuit mathematician and philosopher who ended his life teaching in California. Born in Piedmont in 1816, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1832 and led a seminary at Bertinoro until unrest in 1860 drove him to England. At Stonyhurst he turned to philosophy and wrote three volumes of Realis Philosophia for private circulation.

In 1868 he moved to California, headed St. Ignatius College in San Francisco for three years, and then taught mathematics at Santa Clara until his death in 1892. His best-known work, Molecular Mechanics, treats matter after Boscovich as built from unextended points. Pupils remembered him as a teacher of rare charm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loryma:
Loryma was a small walled town and harbour on the Carian coast, near Cape Cynossema, at the west end of the Rhodian peninsula, twenty Roman miles across from Rhodes. Strabo, Ptolemy, and Livy all name it, yet nothing is known of its history.

Ruins west of Port Aplothiki still show towers, tombs, and ramparts. Its harbour served ships plying the coast between Caria and Rhodes. Church lists place Loryma among the lesser sees under Stauropolis into the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Three bishops are named: George at Constantinople in 680, Anthimus at Nicaea in 787, and Joseph at Constantinople in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massa-maritti:
Massa Marittima, or Massana, was a diocese in Grosseto province, Tuscany, first mentioned in the eighth century. It grew at the cost of Populonia, ancient Etruscan city and chief port, famed for iron, tin, and copper works. Sulla besieged Populonia, Strabo found it already decadent, and Totila, Lombards, and a Byzantine fleet in 817 battered it further.

After that, Populonia's bishops left town and settled at Massa in the eleventh century. Massa became a commune under Pisa's protection in 1226, then allied with Siena in 1307, sparking wars between the republics that brought Massa's decline. First known Populonia bishop was Atellus about 495, then St Cerbonius in 546, protector of the city named in Gregory's Dialogues. Massa bishops included Franciscan general Antonio in 1430, satirist Leonardo Dati in 1467, and Camaldolese Eusebio da Ciani in 1719, who ruled fifty-one years. The see, first Pisa's suffragan, then Siena's from 1458, counted twenty-nine parishes and 68,200 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mobile-alabam:
Mobile, a diocese suffragan of New Orleans, comprises Alabama, 51,540 square miles, and western Florida, 7,281 square miles. It takes its name from Mauvila, the fort and chief city of the Gulf Indians conquered by Hernando de Soto in 1540. De Soto's expedition carried twelve priests, and Mass was certainly offered near present-day Mobile as early as 1540.

From 1540 to 1703 Dominican, Capuchin, and Jesuit missionaries served the region. Its first bishop was Michael Portier, born at Montbrison, France, in 1795, who came to America in 1817 and became first vicar apostolic of Alabama and the Floridas. By 1910 the diocese counted 101 priests, 43 churches with resident priests, and a Catholic population far grown from 17,000 in 1897.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-halm:
Nicholas Halma, French mathematician, was born at Sedan on 31 December 1755 and died at Paris on 4 June 1828. Educated at Paris's College of Plessis, he took Holy Orders and the title of Abbe. In 1791 he became principal of Sedan College. After that school shut in 1793, he moved to Paris and joined the army as a surgeon.

In 1794 he became secretary to the Polytechnic School. He held mathematics chairs at the Prytanée of Paris and geography at Fontainebleau's military school. As librarian to Empress Josephine and the Ecole des Ponts et Chaussées, he taught the empress history and geography. Under the Restoration he became curator at Sainte Genevieve's library and a canon of Notre Dame. In 1808 he continued Velly's History of France for two volumes. His chief work, editing and translating Ptolemy's Almagest into Latin and French, remains a standard for astronomy's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicopolis-arm:
Nicopolis in Armenia Prima, a city Pompey founded for his veterans after beating Mithridates, lay in a well-watered plain below wooded hills. Roads to Comana, Neocaesarea, and Sebasteia radiated from it, and under Nero it became capital of Lesser Armenia and seat of its provincial assembly.

Christianity reached it early, and about 319, under Licinius, forty-five townspeople were martyred and are honored on 10 July. Saint Basil praised its priests as sons of confessors, an earthquake flattened the city in 499, and later writers trace its bishops and churches through Byzantine times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nyssa-cappado:
Nyssa in Cappadocia Prima, a titular see suffragan to Caesarea, is known from maps and bishop lists rather than from any surviving history. Ptolemy, the Antonine Itinerary, Hierocles, and Greek lists of bishoprics all name it, yet its exact site stays uncertain.

Ramsay places it on the south bank of the Halys, ten miles above Kessik Keupru, rejecting Texier's match with Nevşehir. Le Quien names ten bishops, the last a sixteenth-century titular metropolitan, and the town's name still recalls Saint Gregory of Nyssa. Texier wrongly matched it with Nevsehir, while Hamilton noted a village called Nirse or Nissa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oklahoma:
Oklahoma, admitted forty-sixth to the Union, joins former Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory between Texas, Kansas, and New Mexico. Bounded by the Red River in the south, it stretches about 450 miles east to west and 210 north to south across 73,910 square miles.

Rolling land, plentiful streams though none navigable, and a mild climate favor farming even in winter, while buttes link the Ozarks to the Rockies. The entry traces land runs, tribal removals, and statehood, with Catholic missions, parishes, and schools across the new state. Its rivers flow from northwest to southeast, though none is navigable in the strict sense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osma:
Osma is a Spanish diocese covering the civil provinces of Soria and Burgos, with a small part of Segovia. Its seat, Burgo de Osma, holds 3,000 people, while the ancient town of Uxama counts 1,250. The diocese's origin is murky. Some trace it to Saint James the Apostle, others to Constantine's reign, and Florez calls its early existence merely probable.

Bishops of Osma signed Toledo synods from 597 onward, through John, Gregory, Gila, and others into the sixteenth council. After the Arab invasion its bishops lived on as titulars in Asturias. The line was lost until Fernan Gonzalez, Count of Castile, retook Osma and set Silo in the see. Later pages follow the restored diocese, its cathedral, and its bishops down to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panama:
Panama is a Central American republic on the Isthmus of Panama, or Darien, between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Colombia bounds it east, Costa Rica west. It runs about 480 miles long and 37 to 110 miles wide, covers 31,500 square miles, and counts about 420,000 people, mostly of mixed native, Spanish, and African blood.

Canal works drew many North American whites and some 40,000 Black workers from the British West Indies. Bananas lead exports at over 600,000 dollars a year, with coffee, cocoa, rubber, drugs, cabinet woods, and coconuts besides. A state of Colombia until 4 November 1903, Panama then stood independent, while the United States undertook the canal from Colon to Panama City. The entry closes with its dioceses, clergy, and missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parma:
Parma is a city and diocese in central Italy, on its namesake river, a Po tributary winding through a fertile plain of grain, vines, and fine pasture. Silk culture thrives there, with cheese, tobacco, and leather trades besides. Its cathedral, begun in 1060 to replace one burnt two years earlier, was finished in 1074 and dedicated by Paschal II in 1106.

Lombard in style and Latin-cross in plan, with three naves and triple galleries, its sixteenth-century cupola bears frescoes by Correggio and Parmigianino. Choir and sacristy carvings, Gonzate statues, and a fifteenth-century ciborium enrich it further, with Bishop Saint Bernard's tomb in the crypt. The separate octagonal baptistery, begun in 1196 by Benedetto Antelami, and churches like San Giovanni Evangelista and the Steccata complete the tour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quadragesima:
Quadragesima, Latin for the fortieth, names a season of fasting and prayer in imitation of Christ, after Matthew chapter 4. This encyclopedia entry notes that early Christians kept several such seasons: before Christmas, before Easter, and before the feast of Saint John the Baptist. The Greeks kept four, the Maronites six, and the Armenians eight. The great season, before Easter, is the one commonly meant.

It appears in the fifth canon of Nicaea, the sixty-ninth Apostolic Canon, and the Pilgrimage of Aetheria. In the Anglo-Saxon Church, Quadragesima weekday Mass came late in the afternoon, with food taken only near sunset. Under the Roman Rite the weekdays from Ash Wednesday onward rank as major feasts of a lesser kind, with a proper preface and a special oration added at ferial Masses. Duchesne, Kellner and Benger supply the liturgical sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quinquagesima:
Quinquagesima, meaning fiftieth, names the fifty days before Easter in one of its senses. Its first sense is the Sunday before Ash Wednesday, Dominica in Quinquagesima, or Esto Mihi, after its Mass introit's opening words. It ranks as a Sunday of the second class, and violet is the colour of its Mass and Office. For many early Christians it began the pre-Easter fast, and Syrians called it the Sunday of the fast's entrance.

For some it marked the point after which meat was forbidden, giving names like carnis privium, carnevala, the Polish zapustna, and the German herren fastnacht. Where meat abstinence began earlier, this Sunday opened the stricter time without milk or eggs, as the Greeks observed. Quinquagesima also means the joyful season from Easter to Pentecost, from the Saturday after Easter to the Sunday after Pentecost, a time for gladness and reparation for sins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sasima:
Sasima, a titular see in Cappadocia, appears in only three secular documents: the Antonine and Jerusalem itineraries and Hierocles' list. This poor hamlet in a dry region is known to all as the first see of Gregory of Nazianzus, appointed by Basil. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a see its bishop never really held.

Gregory soon left Sasima without exercising episcopal acts there. One reason was Anthimus of Tyana, who claimed jurisdiction, though Greek lists place Sasima under Cappadocia Secunda, while Rome's catalogue keeps it under Cappadocia Prima as a suffragan of Caesarea. Later bishops include Ambrose, who signed a letter to Emperor Leo in 458, Eleusius, an opponent of Chalcedon, and Clement, condemned as a Bogomil about 1143. Today it is the village of Zamzama.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-septuagesima:
Septuagesima, the ninth Sunday before Easter and the third before Lent, takes its name from the Latin word for seventieth. The Greeks call it the Sunday of the Prodigal, from the Gospel they read that day. Latins also called it Dominica Circumdederunt, from the first word of the Mass introit. This entry notes that the name first appears in the Gelasian Sacramentary, and that writers dispute why the day bears it.

It is certainly not the seventieth day before Easter, nor are the following Sundays the sixtieth or fiftieth. One theory makes the season mystically stand for the seventy years of Babylonian captivity. Another treats the name as one of a number series with Quadragesima and Quinquagesima. A third sees it as the earliest day some Christians began Lent. On the eve, the Alleluia falls silent, and the Gloria drops from Sunday Masses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sexagesima:
Sexagesima, the eighth Sunday before Easter and the second before Lent, takes its name from the Latin word for sixtieth. The Fourth Council of Orléans in 541 already knew the name. For Greeks and Slavs it is the Sunday of abstinence from meat, since on it they began, at least in part, to give up flesh.

Latins also called it Exsurge, from the opening word of the introit. The station church was Saint Paul outside the walls of Rome, so the prayer invokes the doctor of the Gentiles. The Epistle, from Paul's second letter to the Corinthians, tells of his sufferings and labors for the Church. The Gospel of the sower sets seed on good and bad ground, while the night lessons continue the story of human wrongdoing, Noah, and the Flood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sidyma:
Sidyma, a titular see in Lycia suffragan to Myra, is named by Ptolemy, Pliny, Hierocles, Stephanus of Byzantium, and Cedrenus. Near the sea and west of Patara, it was built on the southern slope of Cragus, northwest of the Kanthus estuary. Its history is unknown, and its ruins prove it an unimportant place, lying near the village of Doodoorgar, with a theatre, agora, temples, tombs, and some inscriptions.

Le Quien names three of its bishops. Hypatius signed the letter of Lycian bishops to Emperor Leo in 458. Zemarchus attended the councils of Constantinople in 680 and 692. Nicodemus attended Nicaea in 787. Eustathius, present at Seleucia in 359, held both Pinara and Sidyma. The see appears in the Greek lists of bishoprics until the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sodoma:
Giovanni Antonio Bazzi, usually known by his nickname Sodoma, was a Piedmontese and Florentine painter born at Vercelli in 1477 and dead at Siena in 1549. His father was a shoemaker settled at Vercelli. Apprenticed in 1490 to a glass painter from Casale, he went to Milan and fell under Leonardo da Vinci's influence, though he likely never entered Leonardo's studio.

His first important decorative work came in 1503 for an Olivetan convent near Pienza, followed by large frescoes at Monte Oliveto Maggiore, his most notable works. He later decorated the Vatican under Julius II and painted for Agostino Chigi in his Roman villa. Charles V made him a count palatine, and modern judgment rates him far greater and less evil than Vasari's malicious reports allowed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rose-of-li:
Rose of Lima, patroness of America, turned a Lima childhood of prayer and penance into a life of hidden holiness. Born at Lima on 20 April 1586, she took the name Rose at confirmation in 1597, because her infant face had seemed transformed by a mystical rose. She gave herself to prayer, mortification, and devotion to the Infant Jesus and his Mother.

She fasted three times a week, cut off her beautiful hair when vanity assailed her, and laboured with her needle to support her family. Against friends' ridicule and parents' censure she persevered, receiving the Sacrament daily and spending hours before it. She died at Lima on 30 August 1617.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tadama: Tadama was a titular see in Mauretania Caesariensis, of which nothing is known beyond its bishop David. He appears among that province's bishops in the Notitiae episcopatuum of 482. He stands 105th on the list of bishops who went to the Conference of Carthage in 484 and were then exiled by Huneric. The word probatus after his name shows that he died in exile for the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vasco-da-gama:
Vasco da Gama found the sea route to the East Indies. Born at Sines in Portugal's Alemtejo about 1469, he died at Cochin in India on 24 December 1524. His father Estevão, chief magistrate of Sines and commander of Cercal, held high office under Alfonso V. After Bartolomeu Dias returned, João II chose Estevão to lead the next voyage of discovery, but both kings and captains died before it sailed, so Emmanuel I gave the commission to Vasco.

Vasco had already won note early in 1490 by defending Portuguese Guinea colonies against French attacks. Dias had reached the Great Fish River and shown that Africa's coast beyond the Cape turned northward. The entry follows da Gama's voyage round the Cape to Calicut in 1498, his later viceroyalty, and his death in India, a compact life of Portugal's great navigator.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zama:
Zama is the titular see of Numidia, in fact two sees sharing one name: Zama Major and Zama Minor. Zama Minor, represented by Bishop Marcellus at Carthage's conference in 255, is commonly matched to ruins near Furni, southeast of Tunis. Zama Major, or Zama Regia, placed by most historians at Djama village south of Tunis on Silvana's borders, sent Bishop Dialogus to Carthage's conference in 411.

Zama Major's fame rests on Scipio's victory over Hannibal there on 19 October 202 B.C., the battle that settled Africa's fate. A fragmentary inscription proves a colony once stood there, and a decree of A.D. 322 names it Colonia Aelia Hadriana Augusta Zama Regia, confirming the identification. The two Zamas thus pair a minor see known from a single third-century bishop with a major see crowned by Rome's most famous African battle, both now titular memories of Numidian Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zeugma:
Zeugma is the Syrian titular see, suffragan of Hierapolis in the Euphratensis province. A bridge joining the Euphrates' two banks suggested the name, the Greek word meaning a yoke. Pliny says Alexander the Great first built a bridge at this point, no doubt a pontoon bridge, and Seleucus Nicator repaired it. The Parthians habitually crossed the river here, the easiest crossing, and Cassius camped here in his campaign against them under Claudius. In early times two distinct cities, Seleucia and Apamea, stood on opposite banks.

It became customary to say both cities lay on the passage of the Zeugma, and from the first century of our era the name was in current use. Procopius says Justinian walled the city and strongly fortified it. Antioch's sixth-century Notitia lists Zeugma among Hierapolis's suffragans. The site has not yet been found, doubtless near Biredjik.
doe-osti-17014397-progress-towards-micro:
Progress report LA-UR-26-28561, issued September 24, 2026, tracks work on a very precise gamma ray instrument for nuclear fuel work. Katherine Schreiber of Los Alamos and Paige Abel and Ammon Williams of Idaho wrote it. The instrument, HERMES-400, sits at Idaho Materials and Fuels Complex and uses microcalorimeters, ultra cold sensors that read gamma ray energy with unusual sharpness.

In fiscal year 2026 the team finished a final system change meant to improve sharpness, noise resistance, and measuring geometry. A faulty electrical link in the detectors was repaired, and a helium coolant leak was fixed with help from the cryostat vendor. Fresh single isotope test sources also arrived, and measuring them began.
doe-osti-17019157-geometrically-consiste:
Jan Nikl of Lawrence Livermore authored this abbreviated final report, dated September 2026, on a math method for fluid flow simulation. The method serves ALE hydrodynamics, a scheme where the computing mesh moves with the flow, then gets rebuilt and its values remapped, meaning transferred to the new mesh. Standard high order remapping often fails to conserve mass or energy.

The new approach ties remapping exactly to the volume exchanged between mesh cells. That choice conserves total quantities to machine precision while keeping local values within bounds. Tests in a modified test code, Laghos, kept or improved solution quality on standard flow problems. The method still fits the advection based remap used in current lab codes.
doe-osti-17073817-abbreviated-final-repo:
Christopher Hahn of Lawrence Livermore led project 24-ERD-018 on co-designing materials and systems that convert carbon with electricity, reported in October 2026. In a standard electrolyzer, the cathode makes the wanted product, but over 80 percent of the energy is spent at the anode making low value oxygen. The project sought a better anode reaction.

The team studied alcohol oxidation in depth, including how catalyst phases change during use. Machine learning models were built to speed the hunt for new catalysts. A multi scale model, described as a first of its kind, links alcohol oxidation up to plant scale conditions. The result was a paired electrolysis reactor with record low energy input, by the authors account.
doe-osti-2588545-comstock-measure-docume:
Marlena Praprost of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this measure documentation, NREL/TP-5500-95009, dated September 2025. It defines a package scenario inside ComStock, the laboratory's model of the United States commercial building stock. Three upgrades are applied together: ground-source heat pumps, a high efficiency envelope, and LED lighting.

Packages matter because buildings interact with themselves. A better envelope shrinks the heating and cooling load that the heat pumps must serve. Efficient lighting cuts internal heat gains too. The documentation walks the baseline first: existing HVAC systems, windows, walls, roofs, and interior lighting across the stock. Then it specifies the measure. Three heat pump layouts are modeled: central hydronic water-to-water units, packaged water-to-air units, and console water-to-air units. Window replacement and the rest of the envelope package follow. The defined scenario feeds ComStock's public datasets on energy, bills, and emissions.
doe-osti-2588547-comstock-measure-docume:
Marlena Praprost of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this measure documentation, NREL/TP-5500-95005, dated September 2025. It defines a two-part package for ComStock, the laboratory's building-by-building model of the United States commercial stock: geothermal heat pumps paired with a high efficiency envelope, applied across the baseline buildings together.

The logic of the pairing is load first, equipment second. A tighter, better insulated envelope cuts the heating and cooling a building needs, and ground-source heat pumps then meet that smaller load with high efficiency in both seasons. The document's technology summary treats the two halves in turn, then the modeling sections work through the baseline stock's HVAC systems, windows, walls, and roofs before specifying the upgrades. Rate handling is cautious: less reasonable electricity rates are screened out, including noncommercial tariffs and rates whose load profiles fail demand checks. Results feed ComStock's public datasets.
doe-osti-2589518-status-of-multiple-chan:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/60, by Rachel Thomas, Thomas Fanning, Daniel O'Grady, and co-authors, reviews new multi-channel fuel modeling inside a reactor safety code. The code, SAS4A/SASSYS-1, has been used since the late 1960s to study accidents in liquid-metal-cooled reactors. Older runs treated a fuel assembly with fewer, averaged channels.

New options let users split an assembly into channels that mirror its coolant subchannels, such as those in a 19-pin bundle. Added inputs steer how channels share fuel performance data from before an accident starts. Files saved from an earlier run can now seed that starting state, while older models still work unchanged. Unit tests check the new inputs against expected outputs. Analysts gain finer detail on how uneven heating drives an accident.
doe-osti-2589555-informing-arc-divertor-:
A final report on INFUSE award work tackles the divertor of the planned ARC fusion power plant. Jaime Marian at the University of California, Los Angeles, led the work, with Lauren Garrison at Commonwealth Fusion Systems. The divertor is the exhaust region where hot plasma meets solid material. Choosing what that surface is made of, and shaping it well, decides whether the plant survives its own heat.

Work ran from October 2023 to August 2025 and joined several models into one chain. Tasks followed fuel atoms soaking into tungsten and building up over repeated plasma pulses. Other tasks modeled how tungsten grains grow and soften under heat, and the stresses that follow. Findings showed fuel content in the material keeps rising with each cycle, while peak temperatures settle into a repeating pattern. Designers can use the chain to screen materials before cutting metal.
doe-osti-2998651-two-dimensional-silk-cr:
Shuai Zhang, Antonino Tumeo, Chenyang Shi and co-workers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report in September 2025 on two-dimensional silk crystal films for microelectronics. They grew thin layers of silk fibroin, a protein from silk, mixed with clusters called polyoxometalates. Such layers could serve as the active part of a memristor, a device whose resistance remembers past current and suits brain-like computing.

Two cluster types were used to build the layers on graphite, and a scanning probe measured their surface voltage. The clusters tuned the layer so electrons could enter it more easily. Devices built with the silk layer showed repeated, switchable current-voltage curves, unlike plain silk devices. Computer modeling of the curves, using a Bouc-Wen model, supported joint design of device and circuit. The project sets up a design method for protein-based memory devices.
doe-osti-2999080-cyber-physical-tabletop:
Alan Evans, Steve Sweet and Andrew Hahn of Sandia report a cyber-physical tabletop exercise for small modular reactor plants. Charlie Nickerson of Idaho National Laboratory joined them. The report is SAND2025-12429R, dated September 2025. A tabletop exercise talks players through an attack on paper, so weak points surface without touching real equipment. Small modular reactors pair digital controls with nuclear hazards, so both sides must be tested together.

The report first builds a hypothetical plant: its reactor, its safety responses in abnormal events, and its physical protection systems. A design basis threat is set out too, the class of adversary the plant must resist. Then several adversary attack scenarios are played through and judged against that defence. Setup and running of the exercise get their own chapters, so other facilities can repeat the method on their own designs.
doe-osti-3002454-installation-and-demons:
Kory Linton, Ben Garrison, Josh Kendall, Matt Jones, and Nathan Capps document a machine installation in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/3880, dated August 2025. A modified Tormach PCNC 440 milling machine went into the Irradiated Fuels Examination Laboratory hot cell. Inside the shielded cell, it cuts mechanical test specimens from radioactive fuel cladding that staff can only handle with manipulators.

Custom fixtures hold tube samples for axial and ring tension specimens. A printed steel shroud and bowl catch zirconium fines, and a webcam watches the cut. The first irradiated pieces came from the high-burnup 6XV fuel rod. Their dimensions held the target tolerance of plus or minus 0.025 millimeters. Out-of-cell checks confirmed the in-cell work matches ordinary machining scatter. The setup gives the lab an end-to-end specimen workflow.
doe-osti-3011901-a-study-of-emerging-anc: Ancillary service markets in the non restructured western grid are scoped in a short CRADA final report from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, CRD-12-00480, with Doug Arent as technical contact. Rising renewable penetration creates new needs for the services that keep the system reliable. NREL and the University of Colorado Boulder planned to size present and future markets for participants and regulators. The hosted record is brief: it states the aims and a 50,000 dollar in kind commitment, without findings.
doe-osti-3019975-multi-physics-precondit:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-17288, by Malachi Phillips, presents faster solver methods for simulating thermal batteries. Thermal batteries are single-use reserve power sources. A pyrotechnic charge melts their solid electrolyte, and the battery then delivers power. Engineers model these batteries with the Thermally Activated Battery Simulator, known as TABS, but the coupled physics makes the math slow.

Phillips built a hierarchical block Gauss-Seidel preconditioner, a way of breaking the coupled equations into pieces that computers can solve in parallel. It runs through the Teko package in Trilinos and uses multigrid and domain-decomposition solvers for each block of physics. Tests reached 51.3 million degrees of freedom on 2,048 processors, with near sub-second setup and solve times for the electrochemical part. Faster solves allow finer, more detailed battery models.
doe-osti-3022372-employing-macs-vibrant-:
INL report INL/RPT-25-86264 Revision 1, by Jacob Farber and seven colleagues, describes using the MACS testbed and its companion simulator as a stand-in for the MARVEL microreactor. Before the real reactor starts up, its operators and control systems can be rehearsed on a surrogate that behaves like it. That lets startup reactivity tuning and supervisory control procedures be debugged without touching an actual core.

The report details how the surrogate was configured and exercised, and introduces COMMAND, the lab's open-source Python platform for designing and testing advanced reactor controls. COMMAND's modular pieces snap together into dynamic models where candidate controllers can be tested quickly. The broader goal is self-running operation: control methods proven on the surrogate feed directly into the microreactor program's startup testing plans.
doe-osti-3022916-hydrogen-recovery-using:
A final report by Oceanit of Honolulu, under DOE contract DE-FE0032329, covers HALO. The system is meant to recover hydrogen from produced water. That is the oil and gas industry's largest waste stream, at nearly a trillion gallons a year in the United States. HALO drives an arc plasma discharge through the water, splitting out hydrogen while reducing the volume needing disposal, with machine learning in the control loop.

Oceanit, with microwave specialists Sem-Sol and simulation firm ARA, built a Pathfinder prototype to find the concept's performance limits before designing a field pilot. The headline demonstration is that a hydrogen-producing arc plasma can be sustained even in extremely high salinity produced water, which defeats many treatment technologies. Field demonstration slipped, the report notes, because oil and gas cost-share partners were squeezed by market conditions.
doe-osti-3023818-data-driven-atomic-phys:
Derek Mariscal of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory sums up LDRD project 23-ERD work in LLNL-TR-2016846, dated March 2026. The theme is data-driven atomic physics for laser-driven high energy density science. Modern lasers can fire far more often than older ones, and each shot makes data. Machine learning is brought in to turn that flood into faster modeling and discovery.

Mariscal ties the approach to fusion energy research and to rapid model validation for deterrence, nonproliferation, and emergency response missions. Listed publications show the experimental base, including a flexible tape-drive target system for secondary high-intensity laser-driven sources. It was published in the Review of Scientific Instruments in 2023, and high-repetition-rate source work followed in 2024.
doe-osti-3029211-uncertainty-in-dynamic-:
Philip Rae of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this April 1, 2026 report on how much trust a shock Hugoniot deserves. The Hugoniot is the curve of states a material passes through under shock compression, the basic map for weapons and impact physics. Rae's conclusion is a caution: even with the best current techniques for generating that curve, effects from small changes in alloying elements or compressibility are difficult to tell apart.

Timing precision is the bottleneck he quantifies. In experiments with aluminum impactors reaching 7.2 kilometers per second, average spreads were 0.77 nanoseconds for arrival at the first measurement plane and 0.46 nanoseconds at the second. Those spreads are comparable to the half-nanosecond absolute accuracy of a single arrival-time reading, which is exactly why subtle material gaps drown in the noise.
doe-osti-3029212-calculation-of-density-: Q-5 got density-calculated, and this DOE slides cover heat of formation. The pages detail the findings. The chemists get their deck. The formation was heat. The deck was chemist. The Q-5 were formation. The density were calculation. The deck were chemist.
doe-osti-3362600-rdpp-accelerating-diver:
Joseph L. Wilkins of Howard University reports final results under award DE-SC0023511 on widening who does federal climate science. The project served the Energy Department Earth and Environmental Systems Sciences Division. It funded 7 Howard graduate students to work with the department, three of them set to graduate in spring 2025. Two aims carried the work: build partnerships, and build hands-on capability at the university.

The team organized 18 engaged partners, made 3 visits to department facilities, and hosted 5 partner visits to Howard. With NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory staff, they built an air quality data tool now housed in an online information center. Talks took the group to a DC-8 airborne lab workshop, a Harvard air quality meeting, and American Geophysical Union sessions on compound climate hazards and health.
doe-osti-3364104-novel-additive-manufact:
A final report from Florida International University closes DOE FES-RENEW award DE-SC0023647, which ran from February 2023 to January 2026. The project developed additive manufacturing for plasma-facing materials, the tungsten parts that face fusion plasma inside a reactor. PI Bilal El-Zahab led the closing phase with co-PIs Vadym Drozd and Andriy Durygin, with Purdue University and Miami Dade College as partners. Flash sintering, which densifies powders with electric current, was the core technique.

Start-up delays and a change of principal investigator slowed the laboratory work, and the report is candid about both. Undergraduate teams from both schools still completed design projects, including a ceramic 3D printer concept and models of the flash sintering assembly. The award doubled as a research pathway that brought minority-serving-institution students into fusion materials work.
doe-osti-3367000-demonstration-of-contro:
A final report for DOE fusion award DE-SC0022169 demonstrates controlling laser-plasma instabilities with STUD pulses: spike trains of uneven duration and delay. Bedros Afeyan of Polymath Research and Jorge Rocca of Colorado State University wrote it. The experiments ran June 2026 reporting on the ALEPH laser at Colorado State, firing at solid Kapton targets. Instabilities waste laser energy and threaten inertial fusion implosions.

A sub-3-picosecond pump beam struck at 20 degrees after a longer heater pulse made the plasma. Short, separated spikes kept plasma waves in the linear regime, shown by clean quadratic scaling of the second-harmonic signal. Long or overlapping spikes let plasma memory build, and signals turned erratic while Raman and two-plasmon instabilities grew. Spiking, the team concludes, tames instabilities at both the critical and quarter-critical densities.
doe-osti-3377467-case-study-bess-capacit:
Technical report NLR/TP-7A40-99864, dated June 2026, studies how Malawi built skill to plan and run battery energy storage. Andrew Bilich, Kimberly Mazza, Tim Reber, and Jarrad Wright wrote it at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet directed and funded the work. Batteries can firm up a grid short on supply. The skill to site, size, and run them must live in the country, not with advisers.

Local partners anchor the case. ESCOM runs the grid; MERA regulates energy; MUBAS brings university depth. An Alliance-funded resource plan and a battery grid study gave the team tools. Training covered planning software, grid studies, and performance tracking. One session on January 13, 2025 mixed all three partners in person. Next steps named include better load and storage data, shared openly. The case closes with what other countries can copy from Malawi's path.
doe-osti-3401687-phase-1-engagement-summ:
Shannon Anderson and Lis Blanco of the National Laboratory of the Rockies summarize a first phase of community engagement in rural Alabama in report NLR/TP-5400-97876, dated July 2026. The volume is an engagement record, not a technical study: it documents how a workshop was designed, what it produced, and what a follow-up questionnaire returned.

The table of contents shows the shape. Background comes first, then workshop design, the choices about who was invited and how the sessions ran. Results follow in two parts, the workshop's own outcomes and the questionnaire results, so readers can separate what was said in the room from what participants reported afterward. Acknowledgments and an executive summary frame the account. Engagement summaries of this kind are the paper trail that later project phases, and their funding, are built on.
doe-osti-3625674-gigawatt-scale-electrol:
CRADA CRD-24-30440 on gigawatt-scale electrolyzer making closes in National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5900-99777, dated August 2026. Nine lab contacts are printed, led by Peter Rupnowski, Diego Soetrisno, and Guido Bender. The linked award is DE-EE0011303. The goal is a plant in Rochester, New York that can build five gigawatts of proton exchange membrane electrolyzer stacks each year, at set cost targets.

Early work tackled catalyst ink, the liquid that coats each cell layer. Platinum-group particles are dense and settle fast, so layers can vary across a long production run. Studies tracked clumping and settling, then weighed ways to keep inks stable. First loading targets sat near half a milligram per square centimetre, with lower loadings checked for durability. A second task set up checks on incoming ink materials with lab tests. The aim is a written process that can run at full production scale.
doe-osti-3989579-evaluating-geothermal-h:
Nine National Laboratory of the Rockies staff, from Marlena Praprost and Yingli Lou to Lauren Klun, model how geothermal heat pumps would perform across the whole U.S. building stock. Their report, NLR/TP-5500-100158, is dated September 2026. These pumps move heat to and from the ground, heating and cooling homes and workplaces with far less energy than standard gear.

Computer runs stand in for millions of real buildings. One set of runs used 2018 weather and found that about 87 percent of commercial floor area could take a heat pump package. Charts split bill savings by building type and by design: packaged, hydronic, and console units each fit a slice of the stock. Planners can see where ground-source heat pays off first, and what owners might save year by year.
govdocs-archive_org-PaulRassinierCollect:
Paul Rassinier, a French former concentration camp prisoner turned writer, published Debunking the Genocide Myth in French in the postwar years. This English edition came from Noontide Press in 1978. Adam Robbins translated it, and Pierre Hofstetter wrote the introduction. Rassinier questioned the scale and method of the Nazi murder of the Jews.

His study disputes the gas chambers and the accepted death toll, arguing from his own camp experience and selected documents. Historians have refuted his claims in detail, and the book is classed as a founding text of Holocaust denial. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for the study of that literature and its methods.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeisbergManuscr: Harold Weisberg drafted manuscript pages on the investigation of James Earl Ray, the man convicted of killing Martin Luther King Jr. The draft follows a tracing job credited to a man named Jerry. Weisberg treated the Ray case with the same doubt he brought to the Kennedy case. The pages show him shaping evidence and argument before print, in draft form.
gulbadan-humayun-nama:
Princess Gulbadan Begum, daughter of Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire, wrote the Humayun-Nama around 1587. Her nephew Akbar asked her to set down what she recalled of his father, Humayun. Anette Beveridge's 1902 translation is the version here.

Gulbadan tells of Humayun's reign, his exile, and his return to power in India. Because she lived inside the court, she records weddings, births, feuds, and household life that state histories skip. Hers is the only surviving Mughal-era history written by a woman. Its warm, direct voice makes the imperial family feel close and human. She writes of the women's quarters with detail no court historian could match.
joe-strong-the-boy-fire-eater-or-the-mos:
Joe Strong the Boy Fire-Eater is a circus novel for boys by Vance Barnum, published in 1916. Barnum also wrote Joe Strong, the Boy Wizard and Joe Strong and His Box of Mystery. Chapter one, The Vanishing Lady, opens under the big tent of the Sampson Brothers' Circus. Ringmaster Jim Tracy warms up the crowd for Professor Joe Strong.

Tracy boasts that Joe does more than hide eggs or pull rabbits from hats. A lady will sit in full view, then vanish into thin air, and no one will tell how. Joe stands center stage in a spotless suit of white silk tights. The title promises fire-eating as his most dangerous act. Barnum writes the circus as pure wonder for young readers.
lahoma:
John Breckenridge Ellis wrote the novel Lahoma, set in the American West. Its twenty-six chapters open with the touch of a child. A man called Brick makes the next move, then comes flight.

Chapter titles promise a mysterious guest, Red Feather, and getting civilized. A flag of truce and writing home suggest divided loyalties. Later chapters bring fences, a mob, and journey's end. Lahoma herself grows from child to young woman across the tale. Ellis mixes frontier danger with a warm story of raising a girl. Brick's rough frontier ways soften under the child's influence. Growth, not gunplay alone, carries the book to its close.
letters-to-his-son-complete-on-the-fine-:
The complete Letters to His Son gather Chesterfield's whole course of counsel. An editor's note explains old style and new style dating. England's Julian calendar lagged eleven days behind Europe's Gregorian one.

Chesterfield dated letters across that gap with careful marks. From Leipzig study to Paris salons, the letters follow one education. Manners, books, money, and company receive endless, polished advice. Critics have called the teaching cynical; admirers call it honest. Reading the whole run lets each reader judge that famous dispute. Later editors grouped the letters by year for readers. The complete run spans roughly a quarter century of advice.
memoirs-of-the-author-of-a-vindication-o:
William Godwin wrote Memoirs of the Author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. J. Johnson and the Robinsons printed it in London in 1798. Chapter one covers the years 1759 to 1775 of her life.

Godwin holds that the dead of great merit are owed a true account. Calumny and false tales stick to such folk, he argues. A just life story can spur others to walk the same path. No subject, he says, touches the public weal more than hers. The public good, he argues, is bound up with such justice. Honor paid late still teaches the living how to aim.
nasa-tm-19630006259-performance-summary-:
John L. Allen, Owen H. Davis, and Glenn A. Mitchell of Lewis wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-149, in April 1960. It sums up tests of a supersonic air inlet. The inlet was a round, double-cone design built for Mach 3.0 flight. Two cones squeezed the incoming air from the outside.

The team ran the inlet from Mach 3.0 down to Mach 0.8. They tracked pressure recovery, air flow, cowl pressure, and extra drag. A jet engine starves if its inlet wastes pressure at speed. Off-design flight, slower than the design point, strains inlets most. This summary gave engine designers a full map of one bold inlet across its range.
nasa-tm-19680013998-proposed-standards-d:
J. E. Decastra and F. E. Wells, of the Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this February 1968 memorandum, TM X-53692. The pair set out to give missile plumbing leaks a shared, standard language. Under their plan, any worker who finds a leak can describe its size in numbers that others will read the same way.

The work covers the theory behind leak checks and the test gear and steps used to find leaks. Drawings sort threaded and flange leaks into classes, with charts for the ranges between them. An appendix gives the full procedure for describing and estimating leaks in aerospace plumbing. The aim was one clear standard for inspection, testing, and evaluation crews.
nasa-tm-19690018461-a-functional-random-:
Iwao Hosokawa wrote this Goddard preprint, numbered X-641-68-180 and dated May 1969, on a functional random-walk model of the many-particle system. Statistical mechanics follows huge crowds of particles that sit away from equilibrium, still settling toward balance. Hosokawa recasts that hard problem as a kind of random walk, the mathematics of wandering steps.

Transforming his state functional formalism for the BBGKY hierarchy gives the new view, he writes. The basic equation then sits very close to the classic Fokker-Planck form. A slight change turns it into a universal master equation with irreversibility built in. The wandering quantity becomes particle density across the single-particle state space. A general solution is formulated for the weak interaction case.
nasa-tm-19710011693-thermodynamics-of-th:
Lawrence Flax of the Lewis Research Center wrote this theory paper for a spring 1971 physics meeting in Cleveland. It extends the Heisenberg model of a ferromagnet to cover an applied magnetic field. A ferromagnet keeps a lasting magnetic pull, like iron. Near its Curie point, that pull fades as heat turns the material paramagnetic.

Flax worked in the random phase approximation for the uniform case. He studied heat related values near the Curie point. They include magnetization, susceptibility, and how fast magnetization changes with temperature. An outside field lifts magnetization above its zero field value. It also shifts the critical point, and the paper follows both effects.
nasa-tm-19720021198-a-discussion-of-co-a:
Mikio Shimizu of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this discussion in June 1972, numbered X-620-72-209. It treats carbon monoxide and loose oxygen atoms on Venus and Mars. Both planets wear carbon dioxide skies. Sunlight splits that gas into carbon monoxide and oxygen. The puzzle is why the two products do not simply rejoin at once. Shimizu examined chemistry that keeps the balance steady. The paper runs to twenty four pages.

On Venus, carbon dioxide soaks up key ultraviolet light. That shade slows the breakdown of another gas, hydrogen chloride. Chlorine freed there speeds the rejoining of oxygen and carbon monoxide. Related chlorine compounds may tint the Venus haze yellow. Mars shares much of this chemistry in thinner form. The discussion weighed these linked reactions for both planets.
passages-from-a-relinquished-work-from-m:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's "Passages from a Relinquished Work" appeared in his collection Mosses from an Old Manse. The narrator looks back on his boyhood in the home of a village parson who raised him alongside his own three sons. The guardian is remembered under the nickname Parson Thumpcushion, earned by pounding his pulpit cushion while he preached.

The narrator admits the parson's strict rule made his three sons respectable men, while he himself went astray. He tells his own wandering course with dry humour and some regret. The piece reads like a fragment of a life story Hawthorne chose not to finish.
piccolissima:
Piccolissima was translated from the French of Adélaïde de Montgolfier by Mrs. Follen, who signs her preface at Brookline in October 1857. Montgolfier, she notes, was the daughter of the celebrated inventor of balloons. Her fanciful story is, in fact, a little lesson in natural history, and she vouches for the truth of all Piccolissima reports of the insects she meets.

The heroine descends, on her father's side, from the famous Tom Thumb, and on her mother's from a princess who once lodged in a spectacle case. Through her tiny adventures, children learn the manners and customs of insects.
podcast-dannyjones-a2DuoICk4mA:
Young crypto founders who call themselves the Blockchain Boy visit Danny Jones. They run a media firm named Cryptonite. Their partner Michael Sessa joins as chief leader of the venture.

The title claims a teenage fortune made in the metaverse. The guests describe media work tied to coins and virtual worlds. Jones asks how young men built wealth so fast. They explain deals, hype, and timing in a wild market. The episode captures peak crypto confidence, useful now as a record of how that boom sounded from inside. Skeptics will hear plenty to question as well.
podcast-joerogan-BYVQfLi6wMA:
Former television host Steve Hilton joins Joe Rogan for episode 2542. Hilton advised a British prime minister before moving to America. He later worked in California politics and media.

He brings an insider's view of a state at a crossroads. Rogan asks how policy shaped the California dream and its fade. Hilton argues that rules and costs pushed people out. The talk ranges over populism and party failure. Listeners get a British-born analyst reading America's largest state with both love and alarm. His accent only sharpens the outsider's edge he brings.
sakoontala-or-the-lost-ring-an-indian-dr:
Kalidasa wrote Sakoontala, or The Lost Ring, an Indian drama. Sir Monier Monier-Williams translated it into English prose and verse from the Sanskrit. The title page names him as Boden Professor of Sanskrit. It also names him as a fellow of University College and late fellow of Balliol College, Oxford. In his preface to the eighth edition he notes that the translation, first issued in 1855, has gone through seven editions. That record, he admits, might fairly have freed him from the duty of revising it.

Three years before, he heard that Sir John Lubbock had given Sakoontala a place among the hundred best books of the world, and had adopted his version. Monier-Williams therefore went through every line again and compared the translation with the Sanskrit.
sienkiewicz-without-dogma:
