Sienkiewicz turned from vast epics to one man's inner life in Without Dogma, here in English. His hero, a rich and clever aristocrat, keeps a diary of his doubts. He can analyze all things yet cannot quite believe or love with his whole heart.

The diary form lets readers watch a mind trap itself with its own cleverness. Faith, love, and duty all slip through his fingers as he watches. Sienkiewicz called men like him a sign of the age's sickness of soul. The book is his most searching and somber novel, a portrait of modern unbelief from within.
tecumseh-a-drama: Charles Mair wrote Tecumseh as a drama. A quote from Tecumseh's speech to the Osages opens the book. It tells how the first white men came hungry and weak to Native shores. The cast names Tecumseh, chief of the Shawanoes. His brother the Prophet stands beside him. His wife Mamatee and his niece Iena also appear. The American side names General Harrison and General Hull. Harrison was governor of Indiana Territory.
the-darrow-enigma:
Melvin L. Severy's The Darrow Enigma is built as a set of episodes. They are The Episode of the Darkened Room, of the Sealed Document, of Rama Ragobah, of the Parallel Readers, and of the Taletale Thumb. Each episode is split into chapters. A motto asks what we shall say when dream-pictures leave their frames of night and push us from the waking world.

The narrator casts himself as a passive observer rather than an actor in the events. He is a physician, a graduate of a Western university. His practice is now large thanks to a singular blunder into fame: a cure he worked in the now celebrated case he is about to tell. A year earlier, he confesses, he had little enough to do.
the-doctor-s-dilemma: Hesba Stretton's novel The Doctor's Dilemma, printed in New York in 1872 by D. Appleton and Company, is present here only as a title page and contents list. Two parts of plain numbered chapters are named, with no chapter titles at all. The narrative itself is absent here. The two-part frame alone suggests a life split by one hard choice in a doctor's world of sickness and faith.
the-drama:
Henry Irving's The Drama gathers four addresses by the famed actor-manager. The contents name The Stage as It Is, The Art of Acting, and Four Great Actors, with a frontispiece by Whistler. In the first address, given at Edinburgh on November 8, 1881, Irving defends the living stage against those who claim to prize Shakespeare more in print than in play.

Such claims, he says, are cheap pride and fear of the theatre's name. Irving speaks as a working actor for his craft's worth. The talks still show how the stage argued its case.
the-growth-of-english-drama: Arnold Wynne wrote The Growth of English Drama. Wynne held the degree M.A. The Clarendon Press at Oxford printed the book. This impression is dated 1927; the first edition was 1914. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list in six chapters. The chapters run from Early Church Drama and English Miracle Plays through Moralities and Interludes. One treats comedy in Lyly, Greene, Peele, and Nash. One treats tragedy in Lodge, Kyd, and Marlowe. An appendix treats the Elizabethan stage.
the-lone-wolf-a-melodrama: Louis Joseph Vance wrote The Lone Wolf, dated 1914. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The nineteen chapter titles sketch a melodrama's arc: Troyon's, Return, A Point of Interrogation, A Stratagem, Anticlimax, and The Pack Gives Tongue. L'Abbaye, The High Hand, Disaster, Flight, Confessional, Sheer Impudence, and Restitution follow, closing with Unmasked. French place names and the pack imagery suggest a lone operator hunted by a group, though the chapters themselves cannot be read in what is present.
the-moving-picture-boys-at-panama:
Victor Appleton's The Moving Picture Boys at Panama is dated 1915. Its subtitle reads Stirring Adventures Along the Great Canal. Only a frontispiece caption, title page, and contents are present here, so the adventure does not appear. The frontispiece shows earth crashing out from under Joe's feet as he stood on it.

Twenty-five chapters are listed. To the Rescue and On the Brink open the tale, followed by surprises, a delayed letter, and a trip through New York toward Panama. The Little Box and The Secret Conference lead into scenes along the canal, in the jungle, and in Culebra Cut. An emergency dam, a big slide, Gatun Dam, and Mr. Alcando's disappearance fill the closing headings.
the-moving-picture-girls-or-first-appear:
First Appearances in Photo Dramas opens Laura Lee Hope's series The Moving Picture Girls. Only title page and a partial contents list are present here. The sisters' story itself does not appear. Grosset and Dunlap held the 1914 copyright, and the World Syndicate Publishing Company issued the book at Cleveland and New York. A frontispiece caption shows Alice and Ruth holding the stage alone in one scene.

Five chapters are listed with page numbers. An Unceremonious Departure opens at page 1, Russ Dalwood Apologizes at page 11, and The Old Trouble at page 20. Despondency and Replaced close the visible list. Hope's Bobbsey Twins and Outdoor Girls books are advertised on the title page.
the-road-to-mandalay-a-tale-of-burma: B. M. Croker's tale of Burma was first published by Cassell in October 1917 and reprinted three times before a popular edition of 1919, dedicated to a late Royal Munster Fusiliers colonel. Contents move from blinds down and a closed house through kicks and halfpence, clouds, an empty offer, and a monster toward a ship bound for Burma and the land of promise. Here only the title pages, dedication, and opening of the chapter list are present, so the Burmese story itself does not appear.
the-true-woman-a-series-of-discourses-to:
The Rev. J. D. Fulton of Tremont Temple, Boston, published The True Woman in 1869, a series of discourses with Woman versus Ballot added. His preface says the book grew from that lecture's reception: well received by the majority, it met strong opposition from those rejecting the place assigned to woman in the Word of God. Fulton turned more and more to the scriptural argument. He concluded that the campaign to win women the ballot sprang from infidelity to the Word, and to woman herself.

His discourses trace Eve as God made her, the helpmeet; woman as tempter, despoiled of glory; and woman restored through Christ to equality in the church. Fulton writes against women's suffrage from the pulpit at the movement's early height. Historians of that fight will find the opposition's biblical case stated in its own confident terms.
thelma: Marie Corelli's novel Thelma is represented here by a contents list alone, covering Book I and the start of Book II. Chapters run in Roman numerals, paired across two columns without titles. No chapter text follows the list in what is present. Readers can see the book's scale and two-book shape, but none of Corelli's story itself. Only the front listing is present here, so the chapters do not appear.
two-men-of-sandy-bar-a-drama: Bret Harte's Two Men of Sandy Bar survives here through its cast list, headed The Prodigals. Sandy, son of Alexander Morton senior, shares the bill with John Oakhurst, his former partner, who is personating Sandy himself. The cast adds a detective called Capper, an Australian convict named Pritchard, and the Duchess, illegally married to Sandy. Only the dramatis personae are present here, so the drama itself does not appear.
wagner-s-tristan-und-isolde-an-essay-on-:
George Ainslie Hight wrote his essay on Wagner's Tristan und Isolde for readers new to the composer, under lines of Walt Whitman about a victorious song in the night. His preface owns that the pages hold little that is new, and nothing to interest those already at home in Wagner's work. They speak to beginners who want to know what Wagner aimed at and how his operas differ from those that came before.

No English book he knows of, Hight says, gives a beginner that start. An introduction is needed, not because Wagner's works are artificial, but because our minds have been bent by the highly artificial wares of Italian and French opera houses. Against that training, a Wagner drama at first seems strange. Readers get a patient guide to the music drama, its aims, its methods, and its demands on the ear.
